The exam: 70 marks in three parts

Theory20Answer 4 of 5 · 5 marks eachDefinitions, lists, differences, steps. Can be split into (a) (b) (c).

RatingRule
★★★She named it (K-Means / K-Means++, time-series equations), or it was in a quiz and has slide math (MLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation), chi-square, stratified sampling, R²), or it is the main math or theory of a chapter her quizzes never reached (classification metrics, ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic), Bayes, KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours), decision trees, clustering).

Introduction to Data Analytics

Slides: CSE 4261 Week 1 (1–33) · Quiz 1A Q2

TheoryAnalytical★★★

What data analytics is ★★★

  • Data analytics = collecting, cleaning and analysing data to find patterns and make better decisions. In one line: converting data into decisions (data → analysis → insight → decision).
  • Examples: student marks → find weak students; hospital records → predict disease; sales → forecast demand; reviews → measure customer satisfaction.
  • Big data is not only large: it is huge, arrives very fast, comes in many formats, and is hard to manage with traditional tools.
  • Value chain: business problem → decisions needed → analytics → data → big-data technology (Hadoop, Spark, cloud) → insights → decisions, with a continuous-improvement loop.

The 5Vs of big data ★★★

VQuestion it answers · exampleChallenge → solution
VolumeHow much data? Hours of video uploaded to YouTube every minute; years of hospital recordsStorage cost, backup → distributed storage (HDFS: Hadoop Distributed File System), cloud (Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake)
VelocityHow fast is it created and processed? Uber GPS (Global Positioning System) updates, card paymentsData arrives faster than it can be processed → stream processing (Spark Streaming), real-time analytics
VarietyWhat types? Structured (tables), semi-structured (JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), XML), unstructured (images, video, email)Each type needs different processing; hard to integrate → big-data frameworks, integration tools
VeracityCan we trust it? Missing values, duplicates, Age = 250, biasGarbage in, garbage out → cleaning, validation, quality monitoring
ValueIs it useful? Netflix recommendations, fraud detectionMore data ≠ benefit → analytics tied to business goals

Memory line: how much, how fast, what kinds, can we trust it, is it useful.

Three types of data-analytics applications ★★★

  • Monitoring and tracking: watch events as they happen. Uber/Pathao ride tracking, supply-chain GPS/RFID, predictive maintenance (engine sensors flag a failure early), sentiment monitoring.
  • Analysis and insight: find patterns to support decisions. Sentiment analysis, customer segmentation, predictive policing (LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) crime hotspots), election campaigns (targeting undecided voters).
  • New product development: design what customers want. Netflix creates shows from viewing data, Aarong designs from sales data, location-based retail offers.
  • Her food-delivery case: sources app activity, GPS (Global Positioning System), feedback, transactions; uses demand forecasting, delivery optimisation (nearest rider, fastest route), personalised recommendations.
TheoryQuiz 1A · Q2★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Volume is the amount of data generated and stored. Example: a hospital keeps ten years of patient records and MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) scans, many terabytes that need large, scalable storage.

Velocity is the speed at which new data arrives and must be processed. Example: an ICU (Intensive Care Unit) monitor sends every patient's heart rate every second, and an alarm must react in real time.

So volume is a storage problem (how much), while velocity is a processing-speed problem (how fast).

Helping notes

2 marks: one per V, each with an example. Using one setting (a hospital) for both makes the contrast obvious.

Other pairs she could ask: Variety vs Veracity (types vs trust), Volume vs Value (size vs usefulness).

Theory★★★5 marks

Define big data. Explain its 5Vs with an example of each, and give one challenge and solution for any two of them.

Answer, as you would write it

Big data is data so large, fast and varied that traditional tools cannot store or process it efficiently. It is described by five Vs:

  1. Volume: the amount of data (YouTube uploads, hospital archives).
  2. Velocity: the speed it is generated and processed (Uber GPS (Global Positioning System), card payments).
  3. Variety: its different forms: structured tables, semi-structured JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), unstructured images and video.
  4. Veracity: how trustworthy it is (missing values, duplicates, Age = 250).
  5. Value: the useful insight it gives (Netflix recommendations, fraud detection).

Challenges: Volume makes storage expensive → use distributed or cloud storage (HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System), S3). Veracity gives garbage in, garbage out → clean, validate and monitor the data.

Helping notes

1 mark for the definition, 3 for the Vs, 1 for challenge → solution. Draw the 5V table if time allows.

Theory★★★5 marks

Describe the three types of data-analytics applications with one example each.

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Monitoring and tracking: follows events in real time to react quickly. Example: predictive maintenance, where engine sensors warn of a failure before it happens.
  2. Analysis and insight: finds patterns that support decisions. Example: predictive policing, where past crime data shows hotspots so patrols can be planned.
  3. New product development: uses customer data to design new products. Example: Netflix decides which shows to make from what people watch.

The goals are respectively to track, to understand, and to innovate.

Helping notes

Name, purpose, example for each: about 1.5 marks each.

Analytical★★★5 marks

A hospital stores 10 PB (Petabytes) of data, collected very quickly from many sources, but its decisions have not improved. Which V is missing? What should the hospital do?

Answer, as you would write it

The missing V is Value. The hospital has Volume (10 PB), Velocity (fast collection) and Variety (many sources), but data only creates value when it is analysed and used for decisions.

It should: (1) set concrete goals, such as predicting readmissions or bed demand; (2) clean the data so it can be trusted (Veracity); (3) build analytics or ML (Machine Learning) models for those goals; (4) measure whether decisions improved.

Storing data is a cost; using it is what creates value.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A patient's age is recorded as 250. Which V does this break, and why does it matter?

Answer, as you would write it

It breaks Veracity, the trustworthiness of the data. Every model trained on it learns from a wrong value (garbage in, garbage out), so predictions and decisions become wrong.

Fix: validation rules (age must be 0–120), cleaning, and continuous quality monitoring.

2

Data preprocessing: lifecycle, missing values, MLE, noise

Slides: CSE4261 Week 2 (part 1), 1–23 · Word: Data Preprocessing (Week 2) · Quiz 1A/1B Q1 and Q2 · Quiz 2A Q2

Math: MLE (quizzed)TheoryAnalytical★★★

Data vs information ★★★

  • Data = raw, unorganised facts with no purpose yet ("1,099"). Information = processed, organised, meaningful data that supports a decision ("1,099 children enrolled in 2004 had a disability").
  • Qualitative data are words or narratives (interviews, open-ended answers). Quantitative data are numbers (counts, measurements).

The data analytics lifecycle, and why it is iterative ★★★

  • Linear analysis (purpose → question → collect → analyse → interpret → report): simple, but the fixed order limits it. Cyclical analysis has feedback loops and matches real projects.
  • The six phases, each ending with a gate question:
    1. Discovery: learn the business domain, frame the problem, find stakeholders and data sources. "Enough information to draft an analytic plan?"
    2. Data preparation: analytic sandbox, ETLT (Extract, Transform, Load, Transform), learn and condition the data (clean, integrate, transform). "Enough good-quality data to start modelling?"
    3. Model planning: choose methods and variables. "Do I have a good idea of the model to try?"
    4. Model building: train and test. "Is the model robust enough?"
    5. Communicate results to the stakeholders.
    6. Operationalize: pilot, deploy, monitor.
  • It is iterative: a "no" at any gate sends the work back to an earlier phase, and new information keeps arriving.

Analytic sandbox, ETL vs ELT ★★★

  • Analytic sandbox = an isolated workspace holding a copy of real data for exploration, so live production data is never touched.
  • ETL = extract, transform, then load. The sandbox uses ELT (Extract, Load, Transform): load the raw data first, transform later. Raw data is kept: in fraud detection the outliers are the risky transactions, and cleaning first could delete them.
  • Data conditioning = cleaning, normalising, transforming, joining and merging before modelling.

Missing values: MCAR, MAR, MNAR and which imputation to use ★★★

  • Causes: survey refusals, cost (only some patients tested), broken sensors, forgotten entries, privacy. NULL ≠ 0: it means "unknown".
  • MCAR (missing completely at random): unrelated to anything. An internet drop lost random records.
  • MAR (missing at random): depends on another variable. Young people skip the income question.
  • MNAR (missing not at random): depends on the missing value itself. High earners hide their salary. The hardest case.
  • Deleting rows is easy but loses information and biases the sample unless the data are MCAR.
DataImpute with
Roughly normal (height)Mean
Skewed or outliers (income, house price)Median
Categorical (blood group, colour)Mode
Any shape, best fitMLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation): fit the distribution, impute from it

MLE imputation: Gaussian vs log-normal ★★★

\[P(x;\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]
Gaussian density of one value x
  • \(x\)one observed value
  • \(\mu\)mean
  • \(\sigma\)standard deviation
  • \(\pi,\ e\)constants 3.1416 and 2.718
\[\mu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\]
the Gaussian MLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) of the mean is the plain average
  • \(n\)number of known values
  • \(x_i\)the i-th value
  • \(\sum\)add up for i = 1 … n
\[\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^2}\]
the MLE of σ divides by n (not n − 1)
  • \(x_i-\mu\)how far each value is from the mean
  • \(n\)number of known values (divide by n, not n − 1)
\[P(x;\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{x\,\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(\ln x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]
log-normal density: μ and σ are now the mean and SD (Standard Deviation) of ln x; note the extra 1/x
  • \(\ln x\)natural log of the value
  • \(\mu,\ \sigma\)mean and SD of the ln values
  • \(\tfrac{1}{x}\)extra factor from working on the log scale
\[L=P(x_1)\times P(x_2)\times\cdots\times P(x_n)\]
joint likelihood: the model with the larger L fits the data better
  • \(L\)joint likelihood of all the data
  • \(P(x_i)\)density of the i-th value under the fitted model
  • \(n\)number of known values
\[\hat x_{\text{missing}}=\mu\ \ (\text{Gaussian}),\qquad \hat x_{\text{missing}}=e^{\mu}\ \ (\text{log-normal})\]
the imputed value
  • \(\hat x_{\text{missing}}\)the value we fill in
  • \(\mu\)fitted mean (of ln x for log-normal)
  • \(e^{\mu}\)turns the log-scale mean back into the original unit
  • Probability: parameters fixed, data vary ("if μ = 10, σ = 1, how likely is 15?"). Likelihood: data fixed, parameters vary ("I saw 9, 9.5, 11: which μ, σ explain them best?").
  • Gaussian or skewed? Gaussian: values evenly spread, mean ≈ median, no extreme value. Skewed: one huge value (long right tail), mean far above median → take ln x and use log-normal.
Exam recipe (Quiz 1)
  1. Decide Gaussian or skewed, with mean vs median.
  2. Compute μ and σ (on ln x if skewed).
  3. Compute P(x) for each known value.
  4. Multiply them: joint likelihood L.
  5. Impute μ, or eμ for log-normal.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: the values 5, 3, 6, 9, ?, 12, 11 are roughly symmetric. Fit a Gaussian by MLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation), find the joint likelihood and impute the missing value.

Solution
Her worked example★★★

Her Word notes: 40, 50, 70, 80, 4000 and one missing value. Compare a Gaussian fit with a log-normal fit and impute.

Solution
Helping notes

The Gaussian likelihood collapses to about 10⁻²⁰ because 4000 drags μ to 848. The log-normal one is about 10⁻¹⁵, 10,000 times larger, so log-normal wins and the imputed value eμ ≈ 135 is realistic.

MathQuiz 1A · Q1★★★8 marks
Answer, as you would write it

(a) Gaussian. The values 68, 70, 72, 75 are evenly spread with no extreme value; mean 71.25 ≈ median 71.

Helping notes

(b) σ uses ÷ n (the MLE), not n − 1.

(c) Write each P(x) with the formula once, then the numbers. The joint likelihood is the product, a very small number: give it in scientific notation.

(d) The missing score is μ, the most likely value under the fitted bell curve.

MathQuiz 1B · Q1★★★8 marks
Answer, as you would write it

(a) 4000 is an extreme value, so the data are right-skewed. The direct mean (8000/4 = 2000) is pulled far above the typical income (median 1400), so it would be an unrealistic fill. Take ln x and fit a log-normal instead.

Helping notes

(b) μ and σ are computed on the ln values, not on the incomes.

(c) The log-normal formula has an extra 1/x in front. Forgetting it is the classic mistake.

(d) Missing income = eμ, not μ.

Noisy data: attribute noise and class noise ★★★

  • Noisy data = a value is present but wrong or meaningless (Age = 250). Unlike missing data, the value exists.
  • Attribute noise: a wrong feature value (temperature 450 °C, salary −5000), plus missing ("don't know") or incomplete ("don't care") values.
  • Class (label) noise, two kinds. Contradictory examples: the same features carry different labels. Misclassification: one example has the wrong label. Label noise is very harmful in supervised learning.
  • Handling: use robust methods, filter noisy rows out, or polish them (correct or relabel). Data scrubbing: parsing → transformation → deduplication → validation.
TheoryQuiz 2A · Q2★★★4 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Noisy data is data that contains errors or meaningless values: the value is present but wrong, for example Age = 250 or a temperature of 450 °C.

Main types: (1) attribute noise: wrong, missing or incomplete values in the input features; (2) class noise: wrong values in the target label.

Two types of class noise:

  1. Contradictory examples: identical feature values but different labels. Two patients both aged 45 with BP (Blood Pressure) 140, one labelled Diabetes = Yes and the other No.
  2. Misclassification (mislabelled): an example is given the wrong class. A tumour MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) labelled "Healthy", or a cat photo labelled "Dog".
Helping notes

4 marks: definition 1, types 1, each class-noise type with example 1. Adding "filters cannot fix label noise; experts relabel it" is a good finishing line.

TheoryQuiz 1B · Q2★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Data analytics follows a lifecycle (discovery → data preparation → model planning → model building → communicate results → operationalize). Each phase ends with a check, and a "no" sends the work back to an earlier phase: for example, too little good data sends it back to preparation.

New results also raise new questions, and data keep changing, so deployed models are monitored and rebuilt. The work is repeated in cycles rather than done once in a straight line: it is iterative.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the six phases of the data analytics lifecycle. Why is it called iterative?

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Discovery: understand the business problem, stakeholders and available data; form initial hypotheses.
  2. Data preparation: build the analytic sandbox, load data (ELT: Extract, Load, Transform), explore and condition it (clean, integrate, transform).
  3. Model planning: choose the analytical methods and the key variables.
  4. Model building: train the models on training data and test them.
  5. Communicate results: present findings, value and limitations to stakeholders.
  6. Operationalize: run a pilot, deploy, and monitor the model in production.

Iterative: each phase ends with a gate question ("enough good data?", "is the model robust?"); a "no" returns the work to an earlier phase.

Helping notes

Sketch the wheel (her slide above) with arrows going backwards: that earns the "iterative" mark visually.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain MCAR (Missing Completely At Random), MAR (Missing At Random) and MNAR (Missing Not At Random) with examples. Which imputation suits (i) blood group, (ii) house price, (iii) height?

Answer, as you would write it

MCAR (missing completely at random): the missingness is unrelated to any variable. Example: a network failure lost random survey records.

MAR (missing at random): the missingness depends on another observed variable. Example: younger people skip the income question more often.

MNAR (missing not at random): the missingness depends on the missing value itself. Example: people with high salaries refuse to report them.

(i) Blood group is categorical → mode. (ii) House price is right-skewed → median (or log-normal MLE). (iii) Height is roughly normal → mean.

Theory★★★2 marks

Differentiate probability and likelihood.

Answer, as you would write it

Probability: the parameters are fixed and we ask how likely different data are (μ = 10, σ = 1: chance of seeing 15?).

Likelihood: the data are fixed and we ask which parameters explain them best (we saw 9, 9.5, 11: which μ, σ?). MLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) chooses the parameters with the highest likelihood.

MathPredicted★★★10 marks

A landlord records monthly rents (Tk): 8000, 9500, 10000, 12000, 60000 and one missing value.

  1. Is the data Gaussian or skewed? Justify. [1]
  2. Fit a Gaussian and a log-normal model (μ and σ for each). [3]
  3. Compute the likelihood of each value and the joint likelihood under both models. [4]
  4. Which model fits better? Impute the missing rent. [2]
Answer, as you would write it

(a) Right-skewed. 60000 is far above the rest; the mean 19,900 is about double the median 10,000.

Helping notes

Same template as Quiz 1B, but both models are fitted. Conclude with "the higher joint likelihood wins", then impute with that model.

Analytical★★★5 marks

For 40, 50, 70, 80, 4000 the Gaussian joint likelihood is about 8.5 × 10⁻²⁰ but the log-normal one is about 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁵. Explain why, and say which imputation to trust.

Answer, as you would write it

A Gaussian assumes the data are symmetric. The single value 4000 drags its mean to 848 and its SD (Standard Deviation) to about 1576, so the bell curve is flat and wide and every density is tiny; their product collapses.

Taking ln x compresses large values much more than small ones (4000 → 8.29, the others about 3.7–4.4), so the logs are nearly symmetric and a bell curve fits them well. The log-normal therefore gives each point a higher density and a joint likelihood about 10,000 times larger.

Higher likelihood = better model, so trust the log-normal imputation eμ ≈ 135, not the Gaussian's 848, which is larger than four of the five values.

Analytical★★★5 marks

Why can deleting every row that has a missing value be harmful? Why does the analytic sandbox use ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) instead of ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)?

Answer, as you would write it

Deleting a row throws away all its other valid values, so information is lost. If the data are MAR (Missing At Random) or MNAR (Missing Not At Random), the remaining rows no longer represent the population (for example, high earners disappear), so the results become biased. Deletion is only safe for a few MCAR (Missing Completely At Random) rows.

ELT loads the raw data before transforming it. Raw data may hold valuable unusual values (fraud transactions are outliers), and keeping it lets the analyst redo the preparation for a new question. ETL cleans first and can destroy that information.

3

Data cleaning: noise vs outlier, noise-removal filters

Word: CSE 4261 Data Cleaning (p1–11)

TheoryAnalytical★★★

Noise vs outlier ★★★

  • Noise = an erroneous value caused by an error (typing, sensor, transmission, calibration, software, unit conversion). Correct it or remove it.
  • Outlier = a value far from the rest that may be a genuine rare event. Investigate before removing it.
  • Heights 160…170 cm and one 210 cm: 210 may be a basketball player (outlier, keep). 2100 cm is impossible (noise, fix).
  • Noise causes wrong statistics, lower model accuracy, misleading charts and wrong decisions.

The four noise filters ★★★

\[\hat x_t=\frac{x_{t-1}+x_t+x_{t+1}}{3}\]
low-pass (moving average, window 3): each value becomes the mean of its neighbourhood
  • \(x_t\)value at position t
  • \(x_{t-1},\ x_{t+1}\)its left and right neighbours
  • \(\hat x_t\)smoothed output
  • \(3\)window size
\[\frac{12+11+50}{3}=24.33\]
her example: the spike 50 is reduced but still leaks into the output
  • \(50\)the noisy spike
  • \(12,\ 11\)its neighbours
  • \(24.33\)smoothed value, still too high
\[\operatorname{median}\{10,11,12,250,13\}=12\]
median filter: the impulse 250 is ignored completely (the mean would be 59.2)
  • \(250\)the impulse (salt-and-pepper) value
  • \(12\)the middle value after sorting
\[K=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1&-1\\-1&8&-1\\-1&-1&-1\end{bmatrix}\]
high-pass kernel: 8 × centre minus the 8 neighbours
  • \(K\)3×3 kernel (mask) slid over the image
  • \(8\)weight on the centre pixel
  • \(-1\)weight on each of the 8 neighbours
\[8(250)-8(10)=1920\]
one noisy pixel becomes huge: a high-pass filter amplifies noise
  • \(250\)noisy centre pixel
  • \(10\)value of each neighbour
  • \(1920\)filter output
  • Low-pass: passes slow changes, removes rapid spikes. Smooths heart-rate traces; used in MRI/CT, ECG (Electrocardiogram), audio. Limitation: blurs edges.
  • High-pass: passes rapid changes, so it highlights edges (edge detection, sharpening, tumour borders). Limitation: amplifies noise.
  • Median: replaces a value with the median of its neighbourhood. Best for salt-and-pepper (impulse) noise, and keeps edges sharp.
  • Kalman: estimates the true state from noisy measurements by repeating predict and update. Used in GPS (Global Positioning System), robots, self-driving cars, drones, finance.
  • Filters act on feature values only: they cannot fix class (label) noise.
Her worked example★★★

Her Word notes: apply a 3×3 average (low-pass) filter to the inner pixels of this 5×5 patch with a noisy 250 in the centre.

Solution
Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the low-pass, high-pass, median and Kalman filters: what each does and one application.

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Low-pass filter: keeps slow changes and removes rapid fluctuations by averaging neighbours (moving average). Application: smoothing an ECG (Electrocardiogram) or heart-rate signal. It blurs edges.
  2. High-pass filter: keeps rapid changes and removes the smooth background. Application: edge detection or sharpening in medical images. It amplifies noise.
  3. Median filter: replaces each value by the median of its neighbourhood. Application: removing salt-and-pepper noise from images while keeping edges sharp.
  4. Kalman filter: estimates the true state from noisy measurements by repeating predict and update steps. Application: GPS (Global Positioning System) and robot or car position tracking.
Analytical★★★5 marks

A sensor signal 10, 11, 12, 250, 13 has an impulse. Why is a median filter better than a moving average here?

Answer, as you would write it

A moving average adds the spike into its sum, so the spike spreads into the neighbouring outputs. The mean of the window {10, 11, 12, 250, 13} is 59.2, still far from the true level of about 12.

The median only looks at the middle value after sorting: median{10, 11, 12, 13, 250} = 12. One extreme value cannot move it, so the impulse is removed completely and edges stay sharp.

So for impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise, use a median filter.

Analytical★★★4 marks

A high-pass filter turned one noisy pixel into 1920. Why? Is it a good denoiser? Can any filter fix class noise?

Answer, as you would write it

The kernel computes 8 × (centre) − (8 neighbours): 8(250) − 8(10) = 1920. Noise is a sudden, high-frequency change, exactly what a high-pass filter passes, so it is amplified. A HPF (High-Pass Filter) is for edges, not for denoising.

No filter can fix class (label) noise, because filters only change feature values. Wrong labels need relabelling by experts or voting by several annotators.

4

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Booklet: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) p1–35 · Quiz 3A Q1 · Quiz 3B Q3

TheoryAnalytical (quizzed)Math: box plot★★★

What EDA is, why we do it, and its three types ★★★

  • EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis) = examining, summarising and visualising data to understand it before modelling. It comes right after collecting the data.
  • Why: understand the dataset, find missing values and errors, detect outliers, see patterns and relationships, and decide which preprocessing is needed.
  • Univariate (one variable, e.g. CGPA): histogram, box plot, bar chart, summary statistics.
  • Bivariate (two variables, e.g. study hours vs CGPA): scatter plot, correlation, cross-table, line graph.
  • Multivariate (three or more, e.g. house price from area, rooms, age): pair plots, correlation heatmap, PCA (Principal Component Analysis).
  • Steps: objective → inspect rows, columns, types → data quality (missing, duplicates, Age 150) → univariate summaries → distribution and skew → relationships → patterns and anomalies → preprocessing decisions → summarise. EDA is iterative.

Centre, spread and skewness ★★★

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x-\mu)^2}{N}\]
population variance (divide by N)
  • \(\sigma^2\)population variance
  • \(\mu\)population mean
  • \(N\)population size
  • \(x\)each value
\[s^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}\]
sample variance (divide by n − 1)
  • \(s^2\)sample variance
  • \(\bar x\)sample mean
  • \(n\)sample size
  • \(n-1\)degrees of freedom
\[\text{SD}=\sqrt{\text{variance}}\]
standard deviation, in the same unit as x
  • \(\text{SD}\)standard deviation (σ for a population, s for a sample)
\[IQR=Q_3-Q_1\]
spread of the middle 50%, resistant to outliers
  • \(Q_1\)first quartile: 25% of the data lie below it
  • \(Q_3\)third quartile: 75% lie below it
  • Mean (outlier-sensitive), median (resistant), mode (most frequent; works for categories). Range is very outlier-sensitive; the IQR (Interquartile Range) is not.
  • Pairing: symmetric → mean + SD; skewed or outliers → median + IQR; categorical → mode + frequency %.
  • Why n − 1: the sample mean is computed from the same data, so the deviations must sum to 0 and only n − 1 are free (degrees of freedom). Dividing by n would underestimate the population variance.
  • Salaries 30k, 32k, 35k, 40k, 500k: mean 127,400 but median 35,000. Report the median.

Histogram vs bar graph ★★★

HistogramBar graph
DataContinuous numbers (age, income, scores)Categories (department, blood group)
ShowsShape of the distribution: centre, spread, skew, peaksComparison of counts between categories
x-axisNumber intervals (bins)Category names
BarsTouch each other; order fixedHave gaps; order can change

Quick rule: x-axis 0–10, 10–20 … → histogram. x-axis CSE, EEE, CE → bar graph.

AnalyticalQuiz 3B · Q3★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

(a) Histogram. Exam scores are continuous numbers; grouping them into score intervals shows the shape of the distribution, so we can see whether it is symmetric or skewed.

(b) Bar graph. CSE, EEE, CE and Architecture are separate categories; separate bars compare the number of students in each department.

Helping notes

1 mark each: the choice plus one reason (continuous → shape; categories → comparison). A tiny sketch of each is a bonus.

Box plot: five-number summary, fences, outliers ★★★

\[Q_1=\text{median of the lower half},\qquad Q_3=\text{median of the upper half}\]
her method: split the sorted data in two halves
  • \(Q_1,\ Q_3\)lower and upper quartiles
  • \(\text{lower half}\)the values below the median
\[IQR=Q_3-Q_1\]
the length of the box
  • \(IQR\)interquartile range: the length of the box
\[LF=Q_1-1.5\,IQR\]
lower fence
  • \(LF\)lower fence
  • \(1.5\)Tukey's multiplier
  • \(Q_1\)first quartile
\[UF=Q_3+1.5\,IQR\]
upper fence; values beyond a fence are outliers
  • \(UF\)upper fence
  • \(Q_3\)third quartile
  • \(IQR\)Q₃ − Q₁
  • Box from Q1 to Q3, line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values inside the fences, outliers drawn as dots.
  • Why 1.5? Tukey's balance: a smaller multiplier flags normal values, a larger one misses real outliers.
  • Shows centre, middle-50% spread, skew and outliers; best for comparing groups. It hides the individual values and the exact shape.
Her worked example★★★

Her booklet: a batsman's scores in 12 matches are 100, 120, 110, 150, 110, 140, 130, 170, 120, 220, 140, 110. Find the five-number summary, IQR (Interquartile Range), fences and outliers, and draw the box plot.

Solution

Scatter plot and correlation ★★★

  • Construction: (1) choose two numerical variables; (2) independent variable on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis; (3) one dot per (x, y) pair; (4) read direction, strength, outliers and groups.
  • Positive: points rise left to right (study hours vs score). Negative: points fall (price vs demand). None: no direction (shoe size vs exam score).
  • It also shows outliers and visible groups. Correlation ≠ causation.
TheoryQuiz 3A · Q1★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Construction: pick two numerical variables; put the independent one on the x-axis and the dependent one on the y-axis; plot one dot for each (x, y) pair; then read the overall pattern.

Positive correlation: as x increases, y increases (more study hours, higher score). Negative correlation: as x increases, y decreases (higher price, lower demand). No correlation: no clear pattern (shoe size and exam score).

Helping notes

2 marks: construction steps 1, three labelled sketches with examples 1. Label the axes on every sketch.

Theory★★★5 marks

What is EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis)? Why is it done? Explain univariate, bivariate and multivariate analysis with one technique each.

Answer, as you would write it

EDA (exploratory data analysis) is the process of examining, summarising and visualising a dataset to understand it before building models.

Why: to understand the variables, find missing values and errors, detect outliers, discover patterns and relationships, and decide the preprocessing (imputation, scaling, encoding, transformation).

Univariate: one variable at a time, e.g. a histogram of CGPA (Cumulative Grade Point Average). Bivariate: the relation between two variables, e.g. a scatter plot of study hours vs CGPA. Multivariate: three or more variables together, e.g. a correlation heatmap or pair plot for house price, area and rooms.

MathPredicted★★★6 marks

The marks of 10 students are 45, 52, 55, 58, 60, 61, 63, 65, 70, 98.

  1. Find the five-number summary and the IQR (Interquartile Range). [3]
  2. Find the fences and any outliers, and draw the box plot. [2]
  3. Which measures of centre and spread should be reported? [1]
Answer, as you would write it

(c) 98 is an outlier that pulls the mean up, so report the median and IQR.

Helping notes

Sort first. With 10 values, the lower half is the first 5 and the upper half the last 5; Q1 and Q3 are their medians.

Analytical★★★4 marks

Choose a plot and justify it: (a) is blood pressure skewed? (b) number of students per department; (c) study time vs CGPA (Cumulative Grade Point Average); (d) salary spread and outliers across job roles.

Answer, as you would write it

(a) Histogram: BP (Blood Pressure) is continuous and we need the shape of its distribution.

(b) Bar graph: departments are categories; we compare counts.

(c) Scatter plot: two numerical variables; it shows the direction and strength of the relation (add Pearson r).

(d) Side-by-side box plots: they compare the median, IQR (Interquartile Range) and outliers of each job role.

Analytical★★★3 marks

For company salaries the mean is 127,400 but the median is 35,000. What does this say, and which value should be reported?

Answer, as you would write it

The mean is far above the median, so the distribution is right-skewed: a few very high salaries (e.g. 500k) pull the mean up. The median is resistant to such outliers and represents a typical employee, so report the median (with the IQR (Interquartile Range) as the spread).

Analytical★★★2 marks

Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning?

Answer, as you would write it

No. A third variable, hot weather, raises both ice-cream sales and the number of people swimming. Correlation only shows that two variables move together; causation needs a controlled experiment.

5

Statistical analysis and hypothesis testing

PDF: Statistical Analysis and Hypothesis Testing (in the EDA folder), p1–9 · old finals also asked "design a test for two groups"

TheoryAnalyticalMath: t-test★★★

H₀, H₁, α, p-value, Type I and Type II errors ★★★

  • Descriptive statistics summarise data; inferential statistics use a sample to conclude about the population, allowing for sampling uncertainty.
  • μ = true population mean (unknown); x̄ = sample mean; μ₀ = the value claimed under H₀ (from a claim, history or standard, not from the sample).
  • H₀ (null) = no effect: μ = 70. H₁ (alternative) = the effect we look for: two-tailed (μ ≠ 70), right-tailed (μ > 70) or left-tailed (μ < 70). The direction comes from the research question, before seeing data.
  • α (usually 0.05) is fixed before testing; it is the Type I error rate. p-value = P(a result at least this extreme | H₀ true). It is not P(H₀ is true).
  • Decision: p < α → reject H₀ ("significant evidence against H₀"). p ≥ α → fail to reject H₀. Never write "accept H₀" or "proved".
  • Type I error = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α). Type II error = failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β). Power = 1 − β; it rises with larger n and larger effects.
H₀ trueH₀ false
Reject H₀Type I error (α)Correct (power)
Fail to rejectCorrectType II error (β)

The three t-tests ★★★

\[t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}\]
one-sample: one group against a claimed value μ₀; df = n − 1
  • \(\bar x\)sample mean
  • \(\mu_0\)mean claimed by H₀
  • \(s\)sample standard deviation
  • \(n\)sample size
  • \(s/\sqrt{n}\)standard error of the mean
\[t=\frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}\]
paired: the same units measured twice, d = after − before; df = number of pairs − 1
  • \(d\)after − before, for each pair
  • \(\bar d\)mean of the differences
  • \(s_d\)SD (Standard Deviation) of the differences
  • \(n\)number of pairs
\[t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}\]
independent groups (Welch): two separate groups, variances need not be equal
  • \(\bar x_1,\ \bar x_2\)the two group means
  • \(s_1^2,\ s_2^2\)the two group variances
  • \(n_1,\ n_2\)the two group sizes
\[s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}\]
pooled variance, only when equal variances are assumed; df = n₁ + n₂ − 2
  • \(s_p^2\)pooled (combined) variance
  • \(s_1^2,\ s_2^2\)variances of the two groups
  • \(n_1,\ n_2\)group sizes
  • Which test: one sample vs a benchmark → one-sample. The same people twice → paired. Two separate groups → independent (Welch by default).
  • Assumptions: numerical outcome, independent observations, outliers checked, roughly normal data (for paired: the differences) when n is small.
  • Her example: t = 2, df = 15 gives two-tailed p ≈ 0.064 (fail to reject) but right-tailed p ≈ 0.032 (reject). The formula is the same; only the rejection region changes.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: a class claims an average of μ₀ = 70. A sample of n = 16 students has x̄ = 74 and s = 8. Test at α = 0.05.

Solution
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: five students' scores before (60, 65, 70, 58, 62) and after (70, 72, 78, 65, 71) a tutoring programme. Did scores improve? α = 0.05.

Solution
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: CSE scores 75, 78, 80, 74, 77 and EEE scores 70, 72, 74, 69, 71. Is there a difference in mean score? α = 0.05.

Solution
Theory★★★5 marks

Define null and alternative hypotheses, significance level, p-value, and Type I and Type II errors, with an example.

Answer, as you would write it

Null hypothesis H₀: the statement of no effect, e.g. "the mean score is 70" (μ = 70).

Alternative hypothesis H₁: the effect we want evidence for, e.g. μ ≠ 70 (two-tailed) or μ > 70 (right-tailed).

Significance level α: the risk of a Type I error we accept, fixed before the test (usually 0.05).

p-value: the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as ours if H₀ were true. If p < α we reject H₀; otherwise we fail to reject it.

Type I error: rejecting H₀ when it is true (probability α). Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it is false (probability β; power = 1 − β).

Analytical★★★5 marks

60 students: 30 use a new study app and 30 do not; both groups sit the same exam. State H₀ and H₁, list the test steps, and choose the test with a justification.

Answer, as you would write it

\(H_0:\ \mu_{\text{app}}=\mu_{\text{no app}}\)    \(H_1:\ \mu_{\text{app}}\neq\mu_{\text{no app}}\) (use \(\gt\) only if "the app improves scores" was the question from the start).

Steps: (1) fix α = 0.05; (2) check assumptions (independent students, numerical scores, no extreme outliers); (3) compute the t statistic; (4) find p from the t-distribution with its df; (5) p < α → reject H₀, else fail to reject; (6) report the mean difference and its CI (Confidence Interval).

Test: an independent two-sample t-test (Welch): the outcome is numerical, the two groups are different students (so not paired), and the population SD (Standard Deviation) is unknown (so not a z-test).

Helping notes

The previous teacher asked exactly this; it fits her slides too. Marks: hypotheses 1, steps 2, test + reason 2.

MathPredicted★★★6 marks

A university claims students study 20 hours a week on average. A sample of 25 students gives x̄ = 22 hours and s = 5.

  1. State H₀ and H₁ for "the mean is different from 20". [1]
  2. Compute the t statistic and its degrees of freedom. [3]
  3. Decide at α = 0.05. Would a right-tailed test decide differently? [2]
Answer, as you would write it

(a) \(H_0:\ \mu=20\), \(H_1:\ \mu\neq 20\).

(c) Two-tailed p ≈ 0.057 ≥ 0.05, so we fail to reject H₀. Right-tailed (μ > 20) gives p ≈ 0.028 < 0.05, which would reject, but the tail must be chosen before seeing the data.

Analytical★★★4 marks

The same data give a two-tailed p = 0.064 and a right-tailed p = 0.032. Explain. May the researcher switch to one-tailed after seeing this?

Answer, as you would write it

The t statistic is the same in both cases. A two-tailed test counts extreme results in both directions, so its p is twice the one-tailed p (2 × 0.032 = 0.064). At α = 0.05 the right-tailed test rejects H₀ but the two-tailed test does not.

Switching after seeing the data is not allowed: it raises the real Type I error rate above α. The tail must come from the research question before the data are collected.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A report says: "p = 0.03, so H₀ is proved false and the effect is important." Correct both claims.

Answer, as you would write it

A test never proves anything. The correct statement is "at α = 0.05 there is significant evidence against H₀"; p is not the probability that H₀ is true.

Significance is not practical importance: with a large sample even a tiny effect becomes significant. Report the effect size (mean difference, Cohen's d) and a confidence interval.

6

Data transformation and feature engineering

Booklet: Data Transformation (p1–19) · PDF: Feature Engineering (p1–2) · Quiz 2B Q2

Theory (quizzed)AnalyticalMath: scaling★★★

What transformation is, and why we do it ★★★

  • Transformation changes the format, scale, distribution or representation of valid values without changing the observations. Cleaning fixes wrong, missing or duplicate values. Clean data may still need transforming.
  • Why: comparable units, categories → numbers, less right skew and steadier variance, model assumptions, faster optimisation, meaningful distances (KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours), K-Means, SVM (Support Vector Machine), PCA), reproducible pipelines.
  • Scaling matters for distance- and gradient-based models (KNN, K-Means, hierarchical clustering, SVM, PCA (Principal Component Analysis), regularised regression, neural networks). It does not matter for decision trees, random forests and boosted trees.
  • Keep the original variable; record the transformation's parameters and its inverse.

Scaling: min-max, z-score, robust; and data leakage ★★★

\[x'=\frac{x-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}\]
min-max scaling to [0, 1]
  • \(x\)original value
  • \(x'\)scaled value
  • \(x_{\min},\ x_{\max}\)smallest and largest value in the training data
\[x'=a+\frac{(x-x_{\min})(b-a)}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}\]
min-max scaling to any interval [a, b], e.g. [−1, 1]
  • \(a,\ b\)ends of the target range, e.g. −1 and 1
  • \(x_{\min},\ x_{\max}\)training minimum and maximum
\[z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\]
z-score (standardisation): mean 0, SD (Standard Deviation) 1
  • \(z\)z-score: how many SDs (Standard Deviations) x lies from the mean
  • \(\mu\)mean
  • \(\sigma\)standard deviation
\[x'=\frac{x-\text{median}}{IQR}\]
robust scaling: not affected by outliers
  • \(\text{median}\)middle value of the training data
  • \(IQR\)Q₃ − Q₁ of the training data
  • Min-max: bounded and easy to invert, but outlier-sensitive; new values may fall outside [0, 1]. Her waiting times 10–18: σ = √8 = 2.828. Robust scaling: claims 10, 11, 12, 13, 100 → median 12, IQR (Interquartile Range) 2.
  • Data leakage = computing min/max, mean/SD or categories using the test data. Correct order: split → fit the scaler on train only → transform train → apply the same fitted scaler to test → save it with the model.
Her KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) flip (bank example)

Q(30, 60k), A(31, 80k), B(50, 61k). Raw: d(Q, A) ≈ 20,000 and d(Q, B) ≈ 1,000 → B is nearest, because income swamps age. After min-max (age 20–60, income 40k–100k): d(Q, A) = 0.335, d(Q, B) = 0.500 → A is nearest.

Her worked example★★★

Her booklet: scale the exam scores 40, 55, 70, 85, 100 with min-max and with z-score.

Solution
Her worked example★★★

Her booklet: classify Q(30, 60000) by its nearest neighbour among A(31, 80000) and B(50, 61000), after min-max scaling with age 20–60 and income 40,000–100,000.

Solution

Encoding categorical variables ★★★

Variable typeExampleEncoding
Nominal (no order)City, colour, blood groupOne-hot: one 0/1 column per category. Web, Store, Phone → [1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1]
Ordinal (ordered)Low < Medium < High; Poor … ExcellentOrdinal codes 1, 2, 3, 4: keeps the order (gaps not necessarily equal)
BinaryYes / No0 / 1
Target label yHealthy, Benign, MalignantLabel encoding 0, 1, 2: just identifiers, for the target only

Many categories (postcode, product ID): frequency encoding (A, A, B, A, C, B → 0.5, 0.5, 0.333, …), hashing, or target encoding (risk of leakage).

Log and power transforms ★★★

\[y=\ln x\quad(x\gt 0)\]
compresses large values; reduces right skew; use log1p when zeros occur
  • \(y\)transformed value
  • \(\ln\)natural logarithm (base e)
  • \(x\)original value, must be positive
\[T_\lambda(x)=\frac{x^\lambda-1}{\lambda}\ \ (\lambda\neq0),\qquad T_0(x)=\ln x\]
Box-Cox: needs strictly positive x; λ chosen by maximum likelihood on training data
  • \(T_\lambda(x)\)transformed value
  • \(\lambda\)power parameter, fitted by maximum likelihood (λ = 0 means ln x)
  • Log: equal ratios become equal steps (10 → 100 → 1000 becomes 1, 2, 3 in log₁₀). Inverse: x = ey.
  • Box-Cox: only positive values (salary, prices). Yeo-Johnson: also allows zero and negative values (profit/loss, returns).

Feature engineering ★★★

  • Feature engineering = creating new features, or modifying existing ones, using domain knowledge to improve model performance. It often matters more than choosing a fancier algorithm.
  • Types: create (BMI (Body Mass Index) = weight/height²: 80 kg, 1.75 m → 26.1), combine (first + last name), extract (a date → year, month, quarter; a timestamp → hour, weekday; an email → domain), ratio (debt-to-income 40,000/80,000 = 0.50), encode categories.
Data transformationFeature engineeringFeature selection
DoesChanges the form of existing valuesCreates new informationKeeps the best existing features
ExampleMin-max scaling, logBMI from weight and heightDrop Customer ID
AimUsable, comparable dataBetter predictionFewer, relevant features
TheoryQuiz 2B · Q2★★★4 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Feature engineering is the process of creating new features, or modifying existing ones, using domain knowledge so that a model predicts better. Examples: BMI (Body Mass Index) = weight / height² from weight and height; extracting month and weekday from a purchase date; the debt-to-income ratio 40,000 / 80,000 = 0.50.

Data transformationFeature engineering
Changes the format or scale of existing valuesCreates new informative features
Goal: clean, comparable, model-ready dataGoal: better prediction
e.g. min-max scaling of income, log of salary, one-hot of citye.g. BMI, debt-to-income, hour of day
Helping notes

4 marks: FE (Feature Engineering) definition 1, examples 1, difference with examples 2. A two-column table is the fastest way to show "difference".

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain nominal, ordinal and binary variables and how each is encoded. How does label encoding differ from ordinal encoding?

Answer, as you would write it

Nominal: categories with no order (city, colour, blood group). Encode with one-hot: one 0/1 column per category, so no false order is created.

Ordinal: ordered categories (Low < Medium < High). Encode with ordinal codes 1, 2, 3 that keep the order.

Binary: two values (Yes/No). Encode as 0/1.

Label vs ordinal encoding: label encoding gives the target classes integer IDs (Healthy 0, Benign 1, Malignant 2) that mean nothing numerically. Ordinal encoding is for input features whose order is real (Poor 1 … Excellent 4).

MathPredicted★★★4 marks

Patient waiting times (minutes) are 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. (a) Scale them to [−1, 1] with min-max. (b) Compute their z-scores (population σ).

Answer, as you would write it
Analytical★★★5 marks

Why does KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) need scaling but a decision tree does not? Why must the scaler be fitted on the training data only?

Answer, as you would write it

KNN adds the differences of all features into one distance. A feature with a large range (income in thousands) dominates one with a small range (age), so the neighbours are chosen almost by income alone. Scaling puts every feature on the same range so each counts fairly.

A decision tree splits on one feature at a time with a threshold. Scaling keeps the order of the values, so the same rows fall on each side and the tree does not change.

Fitting the scaler on all the data uses the test set's min/max or mean/SD: this is data leakage. The model has indirectly seen the test data, so its test score looks better than it will be on truly new data.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why is ordinal encoding wrong for "City"? Which transform suits profit/loss values that include negatives?

Answer, as you would write it

City is nominal. Codes 1, 2, 3 would invent an order and distances (City 3 "greater than" City 1) that the model treats as real. Use one-hot encoding.

Profit/loss contains zero and negative values, so log and Box-Cox are impossible. Use Yeo-Johnson.

7

Similarity and distance measures

PDF: Similarity and Distance (p1–8) · also Classification Part 2, slides 12–13

Math (often inside KNN or K-Means)Analytical★★★

Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski, Chebyshev ★★★

\[d_{\text{Euclid}}=\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-y_i)^2}\]
straight-line distance
  • \(x_i,\ y_i\)value of feature i for the two points
  • \(\sum_i\)add over all features
\[d_{\text{Manhattan}}=\sum_i |x_i-y_i|\]
city-block distance: walk along the axes
  • \(|x_i-y_i|\)absolute difference in feature i
\[d_{\text{Minkowski}}=\Big(\sum_i |x_i-y_i|^p\Big)^{1/p}\]
p = 1 gives Manhattan, p = 2 gives Euclid
  • \(p\)order of the distance: 1 gives Manhattan, 2 gives Euclid
\[d_{\text{Chebyshev}}=\max_i |x_i-y_i|\]
the largest single difference (Minkowski with p → ∞)
  • \(\max_i\)the largest difference over all features
  • Small distance = similar. Used by KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours), clustering and recommendation.
  • Her A(2, 3), B(6, 6): Euclid 5, Manhattan 7, Minkowski (p = 3) 911/3 ≈ 4.50, Chebyshev 4.
  • Distances depend on scale: (age 20, income 20,000) vs (25, 50,000) are ≈ 30,000 apart because income dominates. After min-max scaling the distance is 0.316 and both features count.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: find the Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski (p = 3) and Chebyshev distances between A(2, 3) and B(6, 6).

Solution

Cosine, Jaccard and Hamming ★★★

\[\cos(A,B)=\frac{A\cdot B}{\lVert A\rVert\,\lVert B\rVert}=\frac{\sum a_ib_i}{\sqrt{\sum a_i^2}\sqrt{\sum b_i^2}}\]
angle between vectors, from −1 to 1; cosine distance = 1 − cos
  • \(A\cdot B\)dot product, the sum of aᵢbᵢ
  • \(\lVert A\rVert\)length of A, √(Σaᵢ²)
  • \(a_i,\ b_i\)i-th components of A and B
\[J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}\]
overlap of two sets, from 0 to 1
  • \(A\cap B\)items in both sets
  • \(A\cup B\)items in either set
  • \(|\cdot|\)number of items
\[\text{Hamming}(A,B)=\#\{i:\ a_i\neq b_i\}\]
number of positions that differ (categorical records)
  • \(a_i\neq b_i\)position i differs
  • \(\#\)count of such positions
  • Cosine compares direction, not length: (1, 2) and (2, 4) give cos = 1. Use it for ratings, word counts, TF-IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency), embeddings.
  • Jaccard: {AI (Artificial Intelligence), Python, Cricket, Coffee} vs {AI, Python, Football, Coffee, Movies} → 3/6 = 0.5. Use it for sets (items bought, movies watched).
  • Hamming: (Red, M, Cotton, Yes) vs (Red, L, Cotton, No) = 2.
  • Scaling affects Euclid, Manhattan and Minkowski strongly; cosine less; Jaccard not at all.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: a user's interest vector is (8, 10, 6, 3, 1). Which reel is more similar by cosine: Cox's Bazar (9, 10, 5, 2, 0) or Football (1, 0, 0, 1, 10)?

Solution
MathPredicted★★★5 marks

A user rated five genres as U = (5, 3, 0, 1, 4). Three movies have genre profiles M1 = (4, 2, 0, 1, 5), M2 = (0, 1, 5, 4, 0) and M3 = (5, 4, 1, 0, 3).

  1. Compute the cosine similarity of U with each movie. [4]
  2. Which movie should be recommended? [1]
Answer, as you would write it
Helping notes

Write the dot product and both lengths for each movie; recommend the largest cosine.

Theory★★★4 marks

Compare cosine similarity and Jaccard similarity: definition, range and when to use each.

Answer, as you would write it

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two numeric vectors, \(\cos=\frac{A\cdot B}{\lVert A\rVert\lVert B\rVert}\); it ranges from −1 to 1 and ignores vector length. Use it for ratings, word-count / TF-IDF vectors and embeddings.

Jaccard similarity measures the overlap of two sets, \(J=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}\); it ranges from 0 to 1. Use it for sets such as products bought or keywords, where only presence matters.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Document d₂ = (6, 0, 4) is document d₁ = (3, 0, 2) written twice. Euclid gives 3.61 (far apart) but cosine gives 1.0 (identical). Which is right for documents, and why?

Answer, as you would write it

Cosine. A document's topic is the direction of its word-count vector, i.e. the proportions of words. Length only reflects how long the document is; doubling every count keeps the direction. Euclid mixes length into the comparison and wrongly calls the two documents different.

8

Data reduction: feature selection, chi-square, sampling

PDFs: Data Reduction part 1 (p1–14), part 2 (p1–19), Numerosity Reduction (p1–3) · Quiz 2A/2B Q1 · Quiz 3A Q2 · Quiz 3B Q1

Math: chi-square, stratified (both quizzed)TheoryAnalytical★★★

Data reduction and its two kinds ★★★

  • Data reduction = a smaller, simpler version of the data that gives almost the same analytical results. Goals: less storage and computation, faster training, less overfitting, easier interpretation and visualisation.
  • Dimensionality reduction removes columns: feature selection keeps a subset of the original features; feature extraction builds fewer new features (PCA: Principal Component Analysis). Numerosity reduction removes rows by sampling. 100,000 × 50 → 100,000 × 10 is dimensionality; → 10,000 × 50 is numerosity.
  • Curse of dimensionality: with many features the space becomes sparse and distances lose meaning, hurting KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours), K-Means and SVM (Support Vector Machine).
  • Feature kinds: relevant (house size), irrelevant (owner's favourite colour, record number), redundant (°C and °F).

Feature selection: filter, wrapper, embedded ★★★

  • Filter: scores each feature with a statistic before any model is trained (correlation, chi-square, ANOVA (Analysis of Variance), mutual information, variance). Fast, simple, model-independent; misses feature interactions.
  • Wrapper: trains a model on different subsets and keeps the best (forward selection, backward elimination). Accurate but slow.
  • Embedded: selection happens during training (Lasso shrinks weights to 0; tree feature importance).
  • ANOVA (concept only): numerical feature vs categorical target; F = between-group variation / within-group variation. Large F → group means differ → useful feature. Mutual information: how much the feature reduces uncertainty about the target; catches non-linear relations.
Feature → targetFilter test
numerical → numericalPearson correlation
categorical → categoricalChi-square
numerical → categoricalANOVA (F)
any, incl. non-linearMutual information
no target usedVariance threshold

Pearson correlation and the variance threshold ★★★

\[r=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum(x-\bar x)^2\,\sum(y-\bar y)^2}}\]
Pearson correlation, from −1 to 1; measures linear relation only
  • \(x,\ y\)paired values of the two variables
  • \(\bar x,\ \bar y\)their means
  • \(r\)correlation coefficient
\[\operatorname{Var}=\frac1N\sum(x-\mu)^2\]
variance threshold: drop features whose variance is below a cut-off
  • \(N\)number of rows
  • \(\mu\)mean of the feature
  • \(x\)each value
\[\operatorname{Var}_{\text{binary}}=p(1-p)\]
variance of a 0/1 feature where p is the share of 1s
  • \(p\)share of 1s in the 0/1 feature
  • Feature vs target: keep large |r| (negative r is still useful); drop r ≈ 0 (House ID 0.02).
  • Feature vs feature: large r means redundancy (Weight–BMI (Body Mass Index) 0.996). Keep the one more related to the target, easier to collect, with fewer missing values.
  • Variance threshold: Internet Access 1, 1, 1, 1 has variance 0 → drop. It ignores the target, and must run before z-scoring (afterwards every variance is 1).
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: Height 1.75, 1.68, 1.82 and BMI (Body Mass Index) 26.1, 21.3, 28.7. Compute Pearson's r.

Solution

Chi-square test of independence ★★★

\[H_0:\ \text{the two variables are independent},\qquad H_1:\ \text{they are associated}\]
always state these first
  • \(H_0\)null hypothesis
  • \(H_1\)alternative hypothesis
\[E_{ij}=\frac{(\text{row total})\times(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}\]
expected count in each cell if H₀ were true
  • \(E_{ij}\)expected count in row i, column j
  • \(\text{row total},\ \text{column total}\)totals of that cell's row and column
  • \(\text{grand total}\)number of all observations
\[\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}\]
add over every cell; O = observed count
  • \(O\)observed count in a cell
  • \(E\)expected count in the same cell
  • \(\chi^2\)test statistic
\[df=(r-1)(c-1)\]
a 2×2 table has df = 1
  • \(df\)degrees of freedom
  • \(r\)number of rows
  • \(c\)number of columns
\[\chi^2_{0.05,\,1}=3.84,\qquad \chi^2_{0.05,\,2}=5.99\]
critical values: reject H₀ if χ² is larger (or if p < α)
  • \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,1}\)critical value for α = 0.05 and df = 1
  • Use it for a categorical feature vs a categorical target (smoking vs disease, gender vs purchase).
  • Reject H₀ → the variables are associated → keep the feature. Her table: smoking χ² 35.20 (p 0.001) select; colour 1.10 (p 0.58) remove.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: 50 students attended a review class (40 passed, 10 failed) and 50 did not (20 passed, 30 failed). Is attending associated with passing?

Solution

Sampling methods (numerosity reduction) ★★★

\[n_h=\frac{N_h}{N}\times n\]
stratified: each stratum gets its share of the sample (Nh = stratum size, N = population, n = sample size)
  • \(n_h\)sample taken from stratum h
  • \(N_h\)size of stratum h
  • \(N\)population size
  • \(n\)total sample size
\[k=\frac{N}{n}\]
systematic: pick a random start, then every k-th member
  • \(k\)sampling interval
  • \(N\)population size
  • \(n\)sample size
\[P(\text{selected})=\frac{n}{N}\]
simple random: everyone has the same chance
  • \(P\)chance that a given member is selected
  • \(n\)sample size
  • \(N\)population size
MethodHowGood / bad
Simple randomEvery member has an equal chance (IDs 1–100, pick 10)Easy, little bias / needs the full list; may miss small groups
StratifiedSplit into homogeneous strata; sample each in proportionEvery subgroup represented / strata must be known
SystematicEvery k-th after a random start (N 1000, n 100 → k 10: 7, 17, 27 …)Quick / biased if the list repeats with a period
ClusterPick a few whole groups at random (10 of 100 schools) and study everyone in themCheap / chosen groups may not represent all
Her quiz trick

The strata feature is the one the research question is about (year of study, age group). Gender, department, blood group and favourite fruit were distractors.

MathQuiz 3A · Q2★★★6 marks
Answer, as you would write it

(a) Stratified sampling. The study compares performance across years of study, and the years have very different sizes (250–500), so every year must be represented in proportion. A simple random sample could under-represent a small year.

(b) Year of Study. The research question is whether year of study influences performance, so the strata must be the years. Gender, department and residence are not part of the question.

(c) Sampling fraction = 300 / 1500 = 1/5.

Helping notes

Check: the stratum samples must add up to n (60 + 90 + 100 + 50 = 300).

MathQuiz 3B · Q1★★★6 marks
Answer, as you would write it

(a) Stratified sampling. Recovery time is compared across age groups of unequal size (300–900 patients), so each group must appear in the sample in proportion.

(b) Age Group. The question asks whether age influences recovery; blood group and favourite fruit are irrelevant to it, and gender is not the variable studied.

(c) Sampling fraction = 400 / 2000 = 1/5.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling. How does stratified sampling differ from cluster sampling?

Answer, as you would write it

Simple random: every member has an equal chance n/N of selection (draw 10 IDs from 100).

Stratified: divide the population into homogeneous strata and sample each in proportion, \(n_h=\frac{N_h}{N}n\) (600 men, 400 women, n = 100 → 60 and 40).

Systematic: compute k = N/n, choose a random start, then take every k-th member (N = 1000, n = 100 → k = 10: 7, 17, 27, …).

Cluster: divide the population into groups, randomly pick a few whole groups and study everyone in them (10 of 100 schools).

Difference: stratified takes some members from every group; cluster takes all members of only some groups.

Theory★★★5 marks

Differentiate dimensionality reduction and numerosity reduction. Explain the filter, wrapper and embedded approaches to feature selection.

Answer, as you would write it

Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of features (columns), by selecting a subset or extracting new ones (PCA: Principal Component Analysis): 100,000 × 50 → 100,000 × 10. Numerosity reduction reduces the number of records (rows), mainly by sampling: 100,000 × 50 → 10,000 × 50.

Filter: rank features by a statistic (correlation, chi-square, variance) before training; fast but ignores interactions. Wrapper: train a model on candidate subsets and keep the best (forward selection); accurate but slow. Embedded: the model selects features while training (Lasso, tree importance).

Analytical★★★4 marks

Weight and BMI (Body Mass Index) have r = 0.996. Should both be kept? Another feature has r = 0 with the target yet clearly matters. How is that possible?

Answer, as you would write it

No. With r = 0.996 they carry almost the same information (BMI is computed from weight), so they are redundant. Keeping both adds multicollinearity and cost without new information; keep the one more related to the target.

Pearson r only measures a linear relation. A U-shaped relation (y = x²) gives r ≈ 0 although y depends strongly on x. Check with a scatter plot or mutual information.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why must constant features be removed before z-score standardisation? Can a low-variance feature still be important?

Answer, as you would write it

After z-scoring every feature has variance 1, so the variance threshold can no longer tell which features were constant; remove them first.

Yes: variance ignores the target. A rare genetic mutation present in 2% of patients has low variance but may strongly predict the disease.

Regression

PDF: Regression (p1–30) · Quiz 3A Q3 · Quiz 3B Q2 · the previous teacher also asked "fit a line + R²"

Math: OLS, R², errorsTheory (quizzed)Analytical (quizzed)★★★

Task, model, loss, optimisation ★★★

  • Regression = supervised learning that predicts a continuous target (price, salary, score, BP) from inputs X.
  • Her table: task regression → model linear regression ŷ = b₀ + b₁x → loss squared error (OLS: Ordinary Least Squares) → optimisation closed-form OLS or gradient descent. "Regression is the task; linear regression is one model."
  • Other regression models: polynomial, decision tree, random forest, KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours), SVR (Support Vector Regression), neural networks.

Simple linear regression by OLS ★★★

\[\hat y=b_0+b_1x\]
the fitted line: b₀ = intercept, b₁ = slope
  • \(\hat y\)predicted value
  • \(b_0\)intercept
  • \(b_1\)slope
  • \(x\)predictor (input)
\[b_1=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}\]
slope: change in ŷ for one more unit of x
  • \(\bar x,\ \bar y\)means of x and y
  • \((x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)\)product of the two deviations
\[b_0=\bar y-b_1\bar x\]
intercept: the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
  • \(b_0\)intercept: ŷ when x = 0
  • \(\bar x,\ \bar y\)means of x and y
\[e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\]
residual: actual minus predicted (e > 0 means the point is above the line)
  • \(e_i\)residual of point i
  • \(y_i\)actual value
  • \(\hat y_i\)predicted value
\[SSE=\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\]
OLS (Ordinary Least Squares) chooses b₀ and b₁ that make this as small as possible
  • \(SSE\)sum of squared errors (residuals)
  • Why square the residuals: positive and negative errors would otherwise cancel; large errors are punished more; the squared loss is smooth with a single closed-form minimum.
  • Her example: b₁ = 5.4 means +5.4 marks per extra study hour; b₀ = 46 is the predicted score at 0 hours.
Closed-form OLSGradient descent
HowDirect formula \(\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\)Repeat \(\beta\leftarrow\beta-\alpha\nabla J(\beta)\)
NeedsNo learning rate, no iterationsLearning rate α, initial values
Use forFew featuresHuge data, neural networks, streaming (SGD: Stochastic Gradient Descent)
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: study hours x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and exam scores y = 52, 56, 62, 68, 73. Fit ŷ = b₀ + b₁x by OLS (Ordinary Least Squares), find the residuals and R², and predict the score for 6 hours.

Solution
TheoryQuiz 3B · Q2★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) is the method that chooses the regression coefficients b₀ and b₁ which minimise the sum of squared residuals, \(SSE=\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\).

Residuals are squared because (1) positive and negative residuals would otherwise cancel out; (2) squaring punishes large errors more than small ones; (3) the squared loss is smooth, so the best line has a simple closed-form solution.

R² and adjusted R² ★★★

\[SST=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2\]
total variation of y around its mean
  • \(SST\)total sum of squares
  • \(\bar y\)mean of y
\[R^2=1-\frac{SSE}{SST}\]
share of the variation in y explained by the model (0 to 1)
  • \(SSE\)variation the model leaves unexplained
  • \(SST\)total variation of y
\[R^2_{adj}=1-\frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-p-1}\]
n = observations, p = predictors; penalises extra predictors
  • \(n\)number of observations
  • \(p\)number of predictors
  • \(R^2\)ordinary R²
  • R² = 0.80 → the model explains 80% of the variation in y. A high R² is not proof of a good model (it may overfit or break assumptions).
  • R² never decreases when a predictor is added, even a useless one (0.82 → 0.83 with shoe size). Adjusted R² can fall (0.81 → 0.80), so it is the fair way to compare models with different numbers of predictors.
AnalyticalQuiz 3A · Q3★★★2 marks
Answer, as you would write it

R² can only stay the same or increase when a predictor is added, even a meaningless one (adding shoe size raised R² from 0.82 to 0.83), so it always favours the bigger model.

Adjusted R² = \(1-\frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-p-1}\) corrects for the number of predictors p: a new predictor raises it only if it improves the fit more than chance would, otherwise it falls (0.81 → 0.80). So adjusted R² shows which model is genuinely better.

Error metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE ★★★

\[MAE=\frac1n\sum|y_i-\hat y_i|\]
average size of the error, in y's unit
  • \(n\)number of predictions
  • \(|y_i-\hat y_i|\)absolute error of prediction i
\[MSE=\frac1n\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\]
squares make large errors dominate; unit is y²
  • \((y_i-\hat y_i)^2\)squared error of prediction i
\[RMSE=\sqrt{MSE}\]
back in y's unit; grows faster than MAE (Mean Absolute Error) when one error is large
  • \(RMSE\)root mean squared error, in the unit of y
  • Never average raw errors: 2, 5, −2 average 1.67 because they cancel.
  • Errors 2, 3, 4 → MAE 3, RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) 3.11 (close). Errors 2, 3, 15 → MAE 6.67, RMSE 8.91 (the big error dominates). Use MAE for robustness and easy explanation; RMSE when large errors are costly.

Her slides: actual scores 70, 80, 90 and predictions 68, 75, 92. Compute MAE (Mean Absolute Error), MSE (Mean Squared Error) and RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error).

Errors e = y − ŷ = 2, 5, −2 are typed into the solver.

Multiple regression ★★★

\[\hat y=b_0+b_1x_1+b_2x_2+\dots+b_px_p\]
several predictors; each b is the effect of its x holding the others constant
  • \(x_1,\dots,x_p\)the predictors
  • \(b_1,\dots,b_p\)their coefficients
  • \(b_0\)intercept
  • \(p\)number of predictors
  • Her example: Score = 20 + 5·Hours + 0.4·Attendance. Hours 4, attendance 80 → 20 + 20 + 32 = 72.
  • Interpretation: +5 marks per extra hour with attendance fixed; +0.4 per attendance point with hours fixed.

Assumptions and residual plots ★★★

  1. Linearity: the relation is straight.
  2. Independent errors: broken by time series and repeated measures.
  3. Homoscedasticity: constant residual spread. A funnel (errors grow with x) is heteroscedasticity: SEs (Standard Errors), CIs (Confidence Intervals) and tests become unreliable.
  4. Normal residuals (not normal X), needed for inference in small samples.
  5. No severe multicollinearity (height in cm and in m): otherwise coefficients become unstable.

Overfitting and underfitting ★★★

Train vs test R²CauseFix
Overfitting0.99 vs 0.55Too complex (x²⁰ polynomial), too many features, little data; it learns noiseCross-validation, feature selection, regularisation, simpler model, more data
Underfitting0.40 vs 0.38Too simple, missing predictorsAdd features, a more flexible model, less regularisation
Good fitHigh and closeCaptures the pattern and generalises to new data

A model's errors on four houses are 2, 3, −4 and 15 (thousand Tk). (a) Compute MAE (Mean Absolute Error), MSE (Mean Squared Error) and RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error). (b) Why is RMSE much larger than MAE here?

Answer, as you would write it

MathPredicted★★★3 marks

Score = 20 + 5·Hours + 0.4·Attendance. Predict the score of a student with 4 study hours and 80% attendance, and interpret the coefficient 5.

Answer, as you would write it

The coefficient 5 means one extra study hour raises the predicted score by 5 marks when attendance is held constant.

Theory★★★5 marks

State and explain the assumptions of linear regression.

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Linearity: y changes linearly with x; a curved pattern breaks it.
  2. Independence of errors: residuals are not related to each other; broken by time series (today's error depends on yesterday's).
  3. Homoscedasticity: residuals have constant spread for all x; a funnel shape means heteroscedasticity and unreliable standard errors.
  4. Normality of residuals: residuals are roughly normal, needed for tests and intervals in small samples.
  5. No severe multicollinearity: predictors are not almost copies of each other (height in cm and in m), otherwise coefficients become unstable.
Helping notes

Draw the three residual plots above to support points 1 and 3.

Theory★★★4 marks

Compare the closed-form OLS (Ordinary Least Squares) solution with gradient descent for fitting a regression model.

Answer, as you would write it

Closed-form OLS computes the coefficients directly with a formula (\(\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\)); it needs no learning rate, no starting values and no iterations, but inverting \(X^\top X\) is expensive with thousands of features.

Gradient descent starts from initial values and repeatedly moves the coefficients against the gradient of the loss (\(\beta\leftarrow\beta-\alpha\nabla J\)) until the loss stops falling. It needs a learning rate and iterations but scales to huge data and is essential for neural networks.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Model A has R² = 0.82 with 2 predictors. Model B adds a third predictor and has R² = 0.83. n = 20. Which model is better?

Answer, as you would write it
\[ R^2_{adj,A}=1-\frac{(1-0.82)(20-1)}{20-2-1}=1-\frac{0.18\times19}{17}=0.7988 \] \[ R^2_{adj,B}=1-\frac{(1-0.83)(20-1)}{20-3-1}=1-\frac{0.17\times19}{16}=0.7981 \]

Model A is better (0.7988 > 0.7981). The third predictor raised R² slightly but not enough to pay for the extra parameter.

Analytical★★★3 marks

The residual plot of a linear model shows a U-shaped curve. What is wrong, and what should be done?

Answer, as you would write it

The linearity assumption is broken: the true relation is curved, so the straight line over-predicts in the middle and under-predicts at both ends in a systematic way.

Add a polynomial term (ŷ = b₀ + b₁x + b₂x²) or transform the variable, then check that the residuals become a random band around 0.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A regression model has R² = 0.99 on training data but 0.55 on test data. Explain and suggest fixes.

Answer, as you would write it

The model is overfitting: it is so flexible (or has so many features) that it learned the noise of the training data, so it does not generalise to new data.

Fixes: use a simpler model or fewer features, regularisation, cross-validation to choose the complexity, or more training data.

10

Classification I: logistic regression, evaluation, Bayes

PDF: Classification Fundamentals Part 1 (58 slides): logistic p1–23, evaluation p24–51, Bayes p52–58 · never quizzed, so expect fresh questions here

Math: metrics, AUC, BayesTheoryAnalytical★★★

Classification, and why a straight line fails ★★★

  • Regression predicts a number (house price $340,000). Classification predicts a label from a fixed set (spam / not spam). Best practice: predict a probability (p = 0.80), then cut it into a label.
  • Linear regression on 0/1 labels fails twice: (1) outputs escape [0, 1] (0 h → −0.30, 10 h → 1.40); (2) one far point (a 15-hour pass) drags the line, moving the 0.5 boundary from 2.5 h to 4 h, so a 3.5 h student is misclassified.
  • We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1, rises in the middle and is flat at both ends: the S-shaped sigmoid.

Logistic regression: sigmoid, boundary, odds ★★★

\[z=w\cdot x+b\]
a linear score, exactly like linear regression
  • \(z\)score (the log-odds)
  • \(w\)weight: how much one unit of x changes z
  • \(x\)input feature, e.g. study hours
  • \(b\)bias (intercept): the score when x = 0
\[p=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\]
the sigmoid squeezes any z into a probability between 0 and 1
  • \(p\)predicted probability of class 1
  • \(\sigma\)sigmoid function
  • \(e\)Euler's number, 2.718
\[p\ge 0.5\iff z\ge 0\iff x\ge -\frac{b}{w}\]
the decision boundary is where z = 0
  • \(-\tfrac{b}{w}\)the input value where p = 0.5
\[\text{odds}=\frac{p}{1-p},\qquad \ln\frac{p}{1-p}=z\]
the log-odds are linear in x
  • \(\tfrac{p}{1-p}\)odds of class 1
  • \(\ln\)natural logarithm
\[\text{odds}_{x+1}=e^{w}\times\text{odds}_x\]
one more unit of x multiplies the odds by e^w
  • \(e^{w}\)odds ratio: the factor the odds are multiplied by per extra unit of x
  • σ(0) = 0.5, σ(2) = 0.88, σ(−2) = 0.12, σ(5) = 0.993. "Logistic regression = linear regression with a sigmoid stapled onto the end."
  • Her model z = 1.5h − 4: boundary h = 4/1.5 = 2.67 hours; each extra hour multiplies the odds by e1.5 = 4.48. The same odds jump moves p from 0.50 to 0.82 (+32 points) but from 0.95 to 0.989 (+4 points).
  • Two features (z = 1.5·hours + 0.8·attendance − 6) → the boundary is a straight line; squared features (z = x₁² + x₂² − 9) → a circle. "Change the features, not the model."

Training loss and choosing the threshold ★★★

\[\text{loss}=-\ln p_{\text{true class}}\]
log loss (cross-entropy): p = 0.99 → 0.01, p = 0.5 → 0.69, p = 0.01 → 4.61
  • \(p_{\text{true class}}\)probability the model gave to the correct class
  • Log loss explodes when the model is confidently wrong. Squared error barely punishes that and, with a sigmoid, has a bumpy (non-convex) surface. There is no closed form, so logistic regression is trained by gradient descent.
  • The threshold is a choice. Cancer screening uses a low threshold (0.1): a missed cancer is catastrophic. Auto-deleting spam uses a high one (0.99): deleting a real email is terrible. Same model, different behaviour.

Confusion matrix and metrics ★★★

\[\text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\]
share of all predictions that are right
  • \(TP\)true positive: positive and flagged
  • \(TN\)true negative: negative and cleared
  • \(FP\)false positive: negative but flagged
  • \(FN\)false negative: positive but missed
\[\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}\]
of those flagged positive, how many really are ("can I trust an alarm?")
  • \(TP+FP\)everyone the model flagged positive
\[\text{Recall}=TPR=\text{Sensitivity}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}\]
of the real positives, how many we caught
  • \(TPR\)true-positive rate
  • \(TP+FN\)everyone who is actually positive
\[\text{Specificity}=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}\]
of the real negatives, how many we cleared
  • \(TN+FP\)everyone who is actually negative
\[FPR=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}=1-\text{Specificity}\]
false-alarm rate (the x-axis of ROC)
  • \(FPR\)false-positive (false-alarm) rate
\[F_1=\frac{2\times\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}\]
harmonic mean: dominated by the smaller of the two
  • \(F_1\)harmonic mean of precision and recall
  • Her example (1000 screened): TP (True Positive) 40, FN (False Negative) 10, FP (False Positive) 20, TN (True Negative) 930 → accuracy 97%, precision 66.7%, recall 80%, specificity 97.9%, F1 0.727.
  • Accuracy trap: a lazy model that always says "no disease" scores 95%. Accuracy only works with balanced classes and equal costs.
  • Optimise precision when false positives are costly (spam deletion, convictions). Optimise recall when false negatives are costly (disease, fraud).
Predicted +Predicted −
Actual +TP 40FN 10
miss, Type II
Actual −FP 20
false alarm, Type I		TN 930

Naming trick: the second word is what the model said (Positive/Negative); the first word says whether it was right (True/False).

Solution

Imbalanced data and SMOTE ★★★

  • 950 negatives vs 50 positives: the model can ignore the rare class. Fixes: oversampling the minority (keeps information, may overfit copies), undersampling the majority (simple, discards data), SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), class weighting.
  • SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) creates new minority points by interpolating between a minority sample and one of its nearest minority neighbours, instead of copying. Risk: unrealistic points where classes overlap.
  • Balance the training set only; validation and test keep the real class ratio. Report recall, precision, F1, ROC-AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) or PR-AUC (Area Under the Precision–Recall Curve), not accuracy.

One model, different thresholds ★★★

  • Lowering the threshold flags more people: recall rises, but false alarms rise too, so precision usually falls. Raising it does the opposite.
  • Her 10 patients: threshold 0.30 → precision 57.1%, recall 100%; 0.50 → 60%, 75%; 0.80 → 100%, 50%.
Her worked example★★★

Her slide 37: ten patients with predicted probabilities A+ 0.95, B+ 0.80, E− 0.70, C+ 0.65, F− 0.55, D+ 0.40, G− 0.35, H− 0.20, I− 0.10, J− 0.05. Find precision and recall at thresholds 0.30, 0.50 and 0.80.

Solution

ROC curve and AUC ★★★

\[\text{ROC point}=(FPR,\ TPR)\ \text{for each threshold}\]
x = false-alarm rate, y = recall
  • \(FPR\)false-positive rate (x-axis)
  • \(TPR\)true-positive rate, i.e. recall (y-axis)
\[AUC=\frac{\#\{(P,N)\ \text{pairs with}\ s_P\gt s_N\}+\tfrac12\#\text{ties}}{n_P\times n_N}\]
pair counting: chance a random positive scores above a random negative
  • \(s_P\)score given to a positive
  • \(s_N\)score given to a negative
  • \(n_P,\ n_N\)number of positives and negatives
\[AUC=\sum (x_2-x_1)\,\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\]
trapezoid rule over consecutive ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) points
  • \(x_1,\ x_2\)FPR (False-Positive Rate) of two neighbouring ROC points
  • \(y_1,\ y_2\)their TPR (True-Positive Rate)
  • (0, 0) flags nothing, (1, 1) flags everything, (0, 1) is perfect, the diagonal is random guessing; a curve below it means "invert the predictions".
  • AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve): 0.5 random, 0.7–0.8 usable, 0.8–0.9 good, > 0.9 strong. It measures ranking, needs no threshold, and compares models; the curve itself is used to pick the operating threshold.
  • Her pair example: 4 P × 4 N = 16 pairs, 12 ranked correctly → AUC 0.75. Her trapezoid example (54 cases) → AUC 0.92 (the slide shows 0.9201 because it rounds the TPRs).
