Bayes' theorem and Naive Bayes ★★★

\[P(C\mid X)=\frac{P(X\mid C)\,P(C)}{P(X)}\]
posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence
  • \(P(C\mid X)\)posterior: probability of class C after seeing X
  • \(P(X\mid C)\)likelihood of X within class C
  • \(P(C)\)prior
  • \(P(X)\)evidence
\[P(+)=P(+\mid D)\,P(D)+P(+\mid\neg D)\,P(\neg D)\]
the evidence, by the law of total probability
  • \(D\)has the disease
  • \(\neg D\)does not have it
  • \(P(+\mid D)\)sensitivity
  • \(P(+\mid\neg D)\)false-positive rate
\[P(C\mid x_1,\dots,x_p)\ \propto\ P(C)\prod_{i=1}^{p}P(x_i\mid C)\]
Naive Bayes: multiply the prior by each feature's likelihood
  • \(x_1,\dots,x_p\)the example's feature values
  • \(\prod\)multiply over all features
  • \(\propto\)proportional to (P(X) is the same for every class, so it is skipped)
\[\hat C=\arg\max_C\ P(C)\prod_i P(x_i\mid C)\]
predict the class with the largest score
  • \(\hat C\)predicted class
  • \(\arg\max_C\)the class that gives the largest value
\[P(x_i\mid C)=\frac{\text{count}(x_i,C)+\alpha}{\text{count}(C)+\alpha k}\]
Laplace smoothing (k = number of values of the feature): no zero probabilities
  • \(\alpha\)smoothing constant (1 = Laplace)
  • \(k\)number of possible values of the feature
  • \(\text{count}(x_i,C)\)rows of class C with that value
  • Base-rate effect: prevalence 1%, sensitivity 95%, false-positive rate 5% → a positive test means only a 16.1% chance of disease, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.
  • "Naive" = features assumed independent given the class: P(free, winner | spam) = P(free | spam) · P(winner | spam). Usually false, but the ranking of classes is often still right. Her spam example: 0.168 vs 0.003 → spam.
  • Variants: Gaussian NB (Naive Bayes) (continuous: age, BP), Multinomial (counts: word frequencies), Bernoulli (present / absent).
Logistic regressionNaive Bayes
TypeDiscriminative: learns P(Y | X)Generative: learns P(X | Y) and P(Y)
IndependenceNot assumedAssumed given the class
TrainingOptimise log lossCount probabilities
StrengthFlexible boundary with enough dataFast; strong for text and small data

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain logistic regression: the sigmoid function, the decision boundary, odds and the training loss.

Answer, as you would write it

Logistic regression is a classification model. It computes a linear score \(z=w\cdot x+b\) and passes it through the sigmoid \(\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\), which maps any z to a probability between 0 and 1.

Decision boundary: predict class 1 when p ≥ 0.5, i.e. when z ≥ 0. For z = 1.5h − 4 the boundary is h = 2.67 hours.

Odds = p/(1 − p); the log-odds \(\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=z\) are linear, so one unit of x multiplies the odds by ew.

Training: it minimises log loss (cross-entropy), −ln p of the true class, using gradient descent; this heavily penalises confident wrong predictions.

Theory★★★5 marks

Define accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 score. When should precision be preferred over recall?

Answer, as you would write it

Accuracy = (TP + TN)/total: the share of all predictions that are right. Misleading on imbalanced data.

Precision = TP/(TP + FP): of everything flagged positive, the share that really is positive.

Recall (sensitivity, TPR) = TP/(TP + FN): of the real positives, the share we caught.

Specificity = TN/(TN + FP): of the real negatives, the share correctly cleared.

F1 = 2PR/(P + R): the harmonic mean of precision and recall; it is high only when both are high.

Prefer precision when a false positive is costly (auto-deleting spam, convicting a suspect). Prefer recall when a false negative is costly (missing a cancer or fraud).

Theory★★★5 marks

What is a ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve? How is AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) computed and interpreted?

Answer, as you would write it

A ROC curve plots the true-positive rate (recall) against the false-positive rate for every possible threshold of a classifier.

(0, 0) means nothing is flagged, (1, 1) everything is flagged, (0, 1) is a perfect classifier and the diagonal is random guessing.

AUC (area under the curve) is computed with trapezoids between consecutive ROC points, or by pair counting: the share of (positive, negative) pairs in which the positive gets the higher score. AUC = probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative: 0.5 is random, 1.0 perfect, above 0.9 strong. It is threshold-free, so it is used to compare models.

Theory★★★4 marks

How can imbalanced data be handled? Explain SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), and why balancing is applied only to the training set.

Answer, as you would write it

Methods: oversampling the minority class, undersampling the majority class, SMOTE, and class weighting (errors on the rare class cost more). Evaluate with recall, precision, F1 or AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) instead of accuracy.

SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique): pick a minority sample, find its nearest minority neighbours, and create a new synthetic point on the line between them. Repeat until the classes are balanced. Unlike copying, it adds variety.

Only the training set is balanced because the test set must reflect real-world class ratios; balancing it would give an unrealistically good score.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain Naive Bayes: Bayes' theorem, the naive assumption and its variants. Compare it with logistic regression.

Answer, as you would write it

Bayes' theorem: \(P(C\mid X)=\frac{P(X\mid C)P(C)}{P(X)}\). Naive Bayes predicts the class with the largest \(P(C)\prod_i P(x_i\mid C)\).

Naive assumption: the features are independent of each other given the class, so the joint likelihood is the product of single-feature likelihoods. It is rarely exactly true, but the class ranking is often still correct.

Variants: Gaussian NB (Naive Bayes) for continuous features, Multinomial NB for counts (word frequencies), Bernoulli NB for binary presence/absence.

vs logistic regression: NB is generative (models P(X | Y) and P(Y)), assumes independence and is trained by counting; it is fast and good for text and small data. Logistic regression is discriminative (models P(Y | X) directly), assumes no independence and is trained by optimising log loss; it is more flexible with enough data.

Analytical★★★4 marks

A cancer-screening model reports 95% accuracy. Why can this be meaningless? Which metric and threshold should be used?

Answer, as you would write it

If 95% of people are healthy, a model that always answers "healthy" already scores 95% while catching no cancer at all. Accuracy hides the errors on the rare class.

A missed cancer (false negative) is far more costly than a false alarm, so the model should maximise recall and use a low threshold (e.g. 0.1). Check precision so alarms stay manageable, and report F1 or PR-AUC (Area Under the Precision–Recall Curve).

Analytical★★★3 marks

A test is 95% sensitive, yet a person who tests positive has only a 16% chance of having the disease. Explain.

Answer, as you would write it

The disease is rare (1%). Out of 10,000 people, 100 are sick and 95 of them test positive. But 5% of the 9,900 healthy people (495) also test positive. So only 95 of 590 positives are sick: 95/590 ≈ 16%.

Sensitivity P(+ | D) is high, but P(D | +) depends on the base rate: false positives from the large healthy group swamp the true positives.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A fraud detector has precision 1.00 but recall 0.02. Its simple average is 0.51. Why is F1 a better summary?

Answer, as you would write it

The detector flagged one transaction correctly but missed 49 of 50 frauds, so it is useless; the arithmetic mean of 0.51 makes it look average.

F1 = 2(1.00)(0.02)/(1.00 + 0.02) = 0.039. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value, so F1 is high only when precision and recall are both high.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why is linear regression unsuitable for a pass/fail classification problem?

Answer, as you would write it

(1) Its outputs are not probabilities: they go below 0 and above 1 (0 hours → −0.30, 10 hours → 1.40).

(2) It is pulled by extreme points: one student who studied 15 hours drags the line and moves the 0.5 cut-off from 2.5 to 4 hours, so a 3.5-hour student who passed is now predicted to fail.

Logistic regression fixes both with the S-shaped sigmoid, which stays between 0 and 1 and flattens at the ends.

Classification II: KNN and decision trees

PDF: Classification Fundamentals Part 2 (70 slides): KNN p1–24, trees p25–70 · Word: Classification Part 2 notes (full tree maths) · she called this lecture "big"; never quizzed

Math: KNN, Gini, entropy, regression treeTheoryAnalytical★★★

K-nearest neighbours: the idea, lazy vs eager ★★★

  • Idea: similar inputs have similar outputs. To classify a new point, look at the K most similar training rows and take a vote.
  • Steps: (1) scale the features, choose K and a distance; (2) compute the distance from the query to every training row; (3) keep the K nearest; (4) majority vote (classification) or average (regression); (5) break ties.
  • Lazy (instance-based): KNN's "training" is only storing the data; all the work is at prediction time (compare with all n rows, O(n·d)). Eager (model-based) learners such as logistic regression fit parameters once and then predict cheaply. "Lazy is not free": 100,000 × 20 means about 2 million operations per prediction.
  • Rank by d² to skip square roots: the order is the same.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides 5–9: S1(3, 5) Fail, S2(4, 3) Fail, S3(4, 6) Fail, S4(3, 8) Fail, S5(6, 7) Pass, S6(7, 6) Pass, S7(8, 6) Pass, S8(7, 9) Pass. Classify q = (5, 6) with K = 1, 3 and 5 (Euclidean).

Solution

Choosing K, breaking ties, distance-weighted votes ★★★

\[w_i=\frac{1}{d_i^2}\]
distance weight: nearer neighbours get a bigger vote
  • \(w_i\)vote weight of neighbour i
  • \(d_i\)distance from the query to neighbour i
\[K\approx\sqrt{n}\]
a starting value for K (n = 200 → try 13 or 15), then tune by cross-validation
  • \(K\)number of neighbours
  • \(n\)number of training rows
  • Her result flips: K = 1 Fail, K = 3 Pass (2–1), K = 5 Fail (3–2), K = 8 just gives the class balance (4–4).
  • K is the bias–variance dial: K = 1 copies noise (low bias, high variance, jagged boundary); a huge K over-smooths (underfits).
  • Use odd K for two classes; tune K with cross-validation, never on the test set.
  • Ties: use an odd K, let the nearest neighbour decide, or weight by 1/d². Weighted K = 3 in her example: Fail 1.000 vs Pass 0.750, which overturns the plain 2–1 Pass.

KNN regression ★★★

\[\hat y=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i\]
plain KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) regression: the mean of the K neighbours' targets
  • \(\hat y\)prediction
  • \(y_i\)target value of neighbour i
  • \(K\)number of neighbours
\[\hat y=\frac{\sum w_iy_i}{\sum w_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{1}{d_i^2}\]
weighted: nearer neighbours count more
  • \(w_i\)weight of neighbour i
  • \(d_i\)its distance
  • \(y_i\)its target value
  • Her rent example: neighbours at d = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 with rents ₹52, 45, 38 → plain mean 45.00, weighted 81.50/1.6944 = 48.10.
  • Predictions are piecewise constant and cannot extrapolate beyond the training targets. If d = 0, return that neighbour's value.

Her slides 21–22: three neighbours at distances 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 have rents ₹52, ₹45 and ₹38 (thousand). Predict the rent with plain and with 1/d²-weighted KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) (K = 3).

Solution
Helping notes

KNN pitfalls: scaling and the curse of dimensionality ★★★

  • Scaling trap (her slide 14): q(25, 60k), A(24, 90k) "won't buy", B(50, 62k) "buys". Unscaled, B is nearest (25.08 vs 30.02); after min-max scaling (age 20–60, salary 30–90k) A is nearest (0.501 vs 0.626). Fit the scaler on training data only.
  • Categories: one-hot for nominal, 0 / 0.5 / 1 for ordinal, Hamming when all features are categorical. Missing values: impute first, never silently put 0.
  • Curse of dimensionality: with many features the nearest and farthest points become almost equally far, so "nearest" loses meaning. KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) also weights every feature equally, so irrelevant features add noise. Fix: feature selection or PCA (Principal Component Analysis).
Her worked example★★★

Her slides 14–15: classify q(25, 60) [age, salary in k] by its nearest neighbour among A(24, 90) "WillNotBuy" and B(50, 62) "WillBuy", after min-max scaling with age 20–60 and salary 30–90.

Solution

Decision trees: anatomy and greedy growth ★★★

  • Root node (the first test), internal nodes, branches, leaves (the predictions), depth. A tree with L leaves is L if-then rules; one prediction follows one path. A leaf stores the majority class and its proportion.
  • Growing = recursive binary splitting: try every feature and cut, keep the purest split, repeat inside each child, stop. It is top-down and greedy (best split now, no look-ahead); finding the optimal tree is NP-hard.
  • CART (Classification and Regression Trees): binary splits with Gini (also regression trees). ID3/C4.5: multi-way splits with entropy and information gain (C4.5 (successor of ID3) uses gain ratio).
  • Candidate splits: binary feature → 1; categorical with k values → \(2^{k-1}-1\) groupings in CART; numeric with m values → m − 1 midpoints.

Gini impurity and choosing the root ★★★

\[\text{Gini}(D)=1-\sum_k p_k^2\]
chance that two random rows of the node have different classes
  • \(D\)the rows in the node
  • \(p_k\)share of class k in the node
\[\text{Gini}_{\text{split}}=\sum_j \frac{n_j}{n}\,\text{Gini}(D_j)\]
weighted by the size of each child
  • \(D_j\)child node j
  • \(n_j\)rows in child j
  • \(n\)rows in the parent
\[\Delta\text{Gini}=\text{Gini}_{\text{parent}}-\text{Gini}_{\text{split}}\]
choose the split with the lowest weighted Gini (largest decrease)
  • \(\text{Gini}_{\text{parent}}\)impurity before the split
  • \(\text{Gini}_{\text{split}}\)weighted impurity after it
  • Pure 8/0 → 0; 6A/4R → 1 − 0.36 − 0.16 = 0.48; worst 4/4 → 0.5 (two classes; with c classes the maximum is 1 − 1/c).
  • Her Word example (8 rows): Employed 0.1875 vs Credit 0.4375 → root = Employed. Her slide example (12 rows): Credit 0.2762 vs Employed 0.3611 → root = Credit.
Her worked example★★★

Her Word notes: grow a depth-2 tree by Gini for Result (Approve/Reject) from Credit (Good/Poor) and Employed (Yes/No).

Solution
Her worked example★★★

Her slides 40–42: 12 loan applications (7 approved, 5 rejected). Which of Credit and Employed should be the root by Gini?

Solution

Thresholds for a numeric feature ★★★

  • Sort the values; take the midpoints between neighbours as candidate cuts; compute the weighted Gini of each "x ≤ cut" split; keep the best.
  • Her example (inside Credit = Poor): incomes 25 N, 33 N, 35 N, 40 N, 52 Y → midpoints 29, 34, 37.5, 46 → weighted Gini 0.300, 0.267, 0.200, 0 → Income ≤ 46 gives two pure children.
Her worked example★★★

Her slide 44: incomes 25, 33, 35, 40 (not approved) and 52 (approved). Find the best threshold by Gini.

Solution

Entropy, information gain and gain ratio ★★★

\[H(D)=-\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k\]
entropy in bits: 8/0 → 0, 6/2 → 0.8113, 6/4 → 0.9710, 4/4 → 1
  • \(p_k\)share of class k
  • \(\log_2\)logarithm base 2, so entropy is in bits
\[IG=H(\text{parent})-\sum_j\frac{n_j}{n}H(D_j)\]
information gain: how much the split reduces entropy
  • \(H(\text{parent})\)entropy before the split
  • \(\tfrac{n_j}{n}\)share of rows going to child j
  • \(H(D_j)\)entropy of child j
\[\text{SplitInfo}=-\sum_j\frac{n_j}{n}\log_2\frac{n_j}{n}\]
grows with the number of branches
  • \(\tfrac{n_j}{n}\)share of rows in branch j
\[GR=\frac{IG}{\text{SplitInfo}}\]
gain ratio (C4.5: successor of ID3): penalises many-valued features
  • \(IG\)information gain
  • \(\text{SplitInfo}\)split information of the same feature
  • Entropy runs 0–1 (two classes) and uses logs (ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3), C4.5); Gini runs 0–0.5 and uses squares (CART (Classification and Regression Trees), cheaper). They usually rank splits the same way.
  • Her 14 applications (8 approved, 6 rejected, H = 0.9852): IG (Information Gain) Credit 0.3960, Co-signer 0.1613, Income 0.1488 → root = Credit.
  • Many-valued trap: Application ID gives 14 pure leaves, so its IG = 0.9852 (the maximum), yet it is useless for new applicants. Gain ratio divides by SplitInfo = log₂14 = 3.807 → GR (Gain Ratio) 0.2588, while Credit has GR 0.4020 and wins.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides 55–62: 14 loan applications with Credit (Good/Poor), Income (High/Medium/Low) and Co-signer (Yes/No). Choose the root by information gain, and check with gain ratio.

Solution

Regression tree ★★★

\[RSS=\sum_{\text{left}}(y-\bar y_L)^2+\sum_{\text{right}}(y-\bar y_R)^2\]
impurity of a split in a regression tree
  • \(\bar y_L,\ \bar y_R\)mean target in the left and right child
  • \(y\)target of each row
\[\hat y_{\text{leaf}}=\bar y_{\text{leaf}}\]
a leaf predicts the mean target of its rows
  • \(\bar y_{\text{leaf}}\)mean target of the rows in the leaf
  • Same search as classification; the best cut gives the lowest RSS (Residual Sum of Squares). Her example (size → price): parent RSS 691.33; best cut Size ≤ 13.5 with RSS 18.67 + 32 = 50.67. Predict size 11 → 23.33, size 17 → 44.
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: house size 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20 and price 20, 24, 26, 40, 44, 48. Find the best split by RSS (Residual Sum of Squares) and predict for sizes 11 and 17.

Solution

Stopping, pruning and missing values ★★★

\[R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha\,|T|\]
cost-complexity: error plus α per leaf (|T| = number of leaves)
  • \(R(T)\)error of tree T on the training data
  • \(|T|\)number of leaves
  • \(\alpha\)penalty per leaf (complexity parameter)
\[\alpha_{\text{eff}}=\frac{R(\text{collapsed})-R(\text{subtree})}{\text{leaves removed}}\]
the α at which pruning that branch becomes worthwhile (weakest link)
  • \(R(\text{collapsed})\)error after pruning the branch
  • \(R(\text{subtree})\)error with the branch kept
  • A tree grown until every leaf is pure memorises the data (12/12 = 100% training accuracy with one-row leaves): overfitting. Training error keeps falling with depth while test error turns up.
  • Pre-pruning stops early (maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf, minimum impurity decrease). Fast, but suffers the horizon effect: a weak split now might have enabled strong splits later. Post-pruning grows the full tree, then cuts branches that don't pay for themselves (CART (Classification and Regression Trees) standard); slower but sees the whole tree.
  • Missing values: impute; surrogate splits (CART: if Credit is missing, use a backup test such as Income > 50k); fractional instances (C4.5 (successor of ID3): send the row down both branches with weights 0.6 / 0.4).
KNNDecision tree
Training / prediction≈ 0 / slow (all rows)Search splits / fast (one path)
InterpretabilityLow (show the neighbours)High (if-then rules)
ScalingEssentialNot needed
BoundaryAny shapeAxis-aligned rectangles
WeaknessCurse of dimensionalityHigh variance, greedy, favours many-valued features
Her worked example★★★

Her slides: subtrees T₀ (error 0.10, 5 leaves), T₁ (0.14, 3 leaves) and T₂ (0.22, 2 leaves). Which subtree is chosen for α = 0.01 and α = 0.05? Find αeff for collapsing T₀ to T₁.

Solution

\(R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|\).

\[ \alpha=0.01:\quad T_0=0.10+0.01(5)=0.15,\qquad T_1=0.14+0.01(3)=0.17,\qquad T_2=0.22+0.01(2)=0.24 \]

Smallest is T₀ → keep the full tree.

\[ \alpha=0.05:\quad T_0=0.10+0.05(5)=0.35,\qquad T_1=0.14+0.05(3)=0.29,\qquad T_2=0.22+0.05(2)=0.32 \]

Smallest is T₁ → prune to 3 leaves.

\[ \alpha_{\text{eff}}=\frac{0.14-0.10}{5-3}=0.02 \]

For α above 0.02, collapsing T₀ to T₁ lowers the cost. α is chosen by cross-validation.

Theory★★★5 marks

Describe the KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) algorithm. Why is it called a lazy learner? How should K be chosen?

Answer, as you would write it

Algorithm: (1) scale the features and choose K and a distance measure; (2) compute the distance from the new point to every training point; (3) select the K nearest; (4) predict by majority vote (classification) or by the mean of their targets (regression); (5) break ties with odd K, the nearest neighbour or 1/d² weights.

Lazy: KNN builds no model during training; it only stores the data and does all the work at prediction time by comparing with every row. Eager learners (logistic regression) fit parameters first and predict quickly.

Choosing K: small K follows noise (high variance); large K over-smooths (high bias). Start near √n, use an odd K for two classes, and pick the K with the lowest cross-validation error.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the parts of a decision tree and how a tree is grown.

Answer, as you would write it

Parts: the root node holds the first test on the whole data; internal nodes hold further tests; branches are the outcomes of a test; leaves hold the predicted class (or mean value); depth is the longest root-to-leaf path.

Growing (recursive binary splitting): at a node, try every feature and every possible cut, measure the impurity of the children (Gini, entropy or RSS), and choose the split that reduces impurity the most. Repeat inside each child until a stopping rule holds (pure node, maximum depth, too few samples). The method is greedy: it picks the best split now without looking ahead.

Theory★★★5 marks

Compare Gini impurity and entropy. Why can information gain be misleading, and how does gain ratio fix it?

Answer, as you would write it

Gini \(=1-\sum p_k^2\) ranges 0–0.5 for two classes and uses squares (CART: Classification and Regression Trees). Entropy \(=-\sum p_k\log_2 p_k\) ranges 0–1 and uses logarithms (ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3), C4.5). Both are 0 for a pure node and largest for a 50/50 node, and they usually choose the same split; Gini is cheaper to compute.

Problem with IG (Information Gain): it favours features with many values. An Application ID gives one pure leaf per row, so its IG is the maximum (0.9852), although it is useless for new data.

Gain ratio \(=\frac{IG}{\text{SplitInfo}}\) divides by the split information, which is large for many branches (log₂14 = 3.81). The ID's GR (Gain Ratio) falls to 0.26, and Credit (GR 0.40) is chosen.

Theory★★★4 marks

Compare pre-pruning and post-pruning. What is the horizon effect?

Answer, as you would write it

Pre-pruning stops growing early using limits such as maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf or minimum impurity decrease. It is fast, but may stop too soon.

Post-pruning grows the full tree and then removes branches that don't improve validation performance, using cost-complexity \(R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|\). It is slower but sees the whole tree.

Horizon effect: pre-pruning may reject a split that looks weak now even though it would enable very good splits below it.

Theory★★★5 marks

Compare KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) and decision trees.

Answer, as you would write it
KNNDecision tree
LearningLazy: stores the dataEager: learns splits
Prediction costHigh: compares with every rowLow: follows one path
InterpretabilityLowHigh: if-then rules
Feature scalingEssentialNot needed
Decision boundaryAny shapeAxis-aligned rectangles
Main weaknessCurse of dimensionality, irrelevant featuresOverfitting, high variance
Analytical★★★3 marks

In a loan dataset, "Application ID" has the highest information gain. Should it be the root? What fixes this?

Answer, as you would write it

No. Every ID is unique, so splitting on it gives one pure leaf per application and the maximum IG (Information Gain) (0.9852). But it only memorises the training rows and says nothing about a new applicant: it is pure overfitting.

Information gain is biased towards many-valued features. Gain ratio divides IG by SplitInfo (log₂14 = 3.81 for 14 values), which drops the ID to 0.26 so Credit (0.40) becomes the root. Removing identifier columns before training also fixes it.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A decision tree reaches 100% training accuracy but performs poorly on test data. Why, and how should it be fixed?

Answer, as you would write it

The tree kept splitting until every leaf was pure, often with a single row each, so it memorised noise in the training data (overfitting, high variance) and cannot generalise.

Fix: pre-pruning limits (maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf), post-pruning with cost-complexity α chosen by cross-validation, or an ensemble such as a random forest.

Analytical★★★3 marks

KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) predicts Fail for K = 1, Pass for K = 3 and Fail for K = 5. What does this tell us, and why avoid an even K?

Answer, as you would write it

The query lies near the class boundary: the single nearest point is Fail, the next two are Pass, and more Fail points appear a little further away. Small K reacts to local noise; large K drifts towards the overall class balance. The right K should be chosen by cross-validation.

An even K can tie (K = 2 gives 1–1; K = 8 gives 4–4), so use an odd K for two classes or weight votes by distance.

Analytical★★★3 marks

With K = 3 the plain vote is Pass (2–1), but the 1/d²-weighted vote is Fail. Explain.

Answer, as you would write it

The single Fail neighbour S3 is very close (d² = 1, weight 1.000), while the two Pass neighbours are further (d² = 2 and 4, weights 0.500 and 0.250, total 0.750). Weighting trusts close neighbours more, so the one very close Fail outweighs two farther Passes: Fail 1.000 vs Pass 0.750.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why does KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) perform badly when there are hundreds of features?

Answer, as you would write it

In high dimensions the data become sparse and all distances become almost equal (the nearest point is barely nearer than the farthest), so "nearest neighbour" loses meaning: the curse of dimensionality. KNN also weights every feature equally, so many irrelevant features drown the useful ones.

Fix: feature selection or dimensionality reduction (PCA: Principal Component Analysis) before KNN.

Analytical★★★3 marks

The true class boundary is a diagonal line x₁ = x₂. Why does a decision tree need many splits to model it?

Answer, as you would write it

Each tree split tests one feature against a threshold, so every boundary piece is parallel to an axis. A diagonal can only be approximated by a staircase of many small horizontal and vertical steps, giving a deep tree that tends to overfit. KNN (K-Nearest Neighbours) or logistic regression can draw the diagonal directly.

Unsupervised learning: K-Means, choosing K, hierarchical, Apriori, PCA, semi-supervised, RL

PPTX: Unsupervised Learning (86 slides) · Word: K-Means and K-Means++ notes, WCSS notes · she promised: "K-Means or K-Means++, one math will come"

Math: K-Means / K-Means++ (near-certain)TheoryAnalytical★★★

Supervised vs unsupervised learning ★★★

  • Supervised: data {(x, y)} with labels; learn f(x) ≈ y; success is measured against the true labels (classification, regression).
  • Unsupervised: data {x} only; discover structure using a proxy objective (compactness, density, variance); success is judged indirectly.
  • Kinds: clustering (K-Means, hierarchical, DBSCAN), dimensionality reduction (PCA: Principal Component Analysis), association mining (Apriori, FP-Growth), density estimation. Uses: labels are expensive, exploring data, anomaly detection, compression.

K-Means (Lloyd's algorithm) ★★★

\[d(x,\mu)=\sqrt{(x_1-\mu_1)^2+(x_2-\mu_2)^2}\]
Euclidean distance from a point to a centroid
  • \(x=(x_1,x_2)\)a data point
  • \(\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2)\)a centroid
\[\mu_i=\frac{1}{|C_i|}\sum_{x\in C_i}x\]
update: each centroid moves to the mean of its points
  • \(C_i\)cluster i
  • \(|C_i|\)number of points in cluster i
  • \(\mu_i\)centroid (mean) of cluster i
\[J=\text{WCSS}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ \sum_{x\in C_i}\lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2\]
within-cluster sum of squares: what K-Means makes small
  • \(k\)number of clusters
  • \(\lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2\)squared distance from x to its centroid
  1. Initialise k centroids (given points, or K-Means++).
  2. Assign every point to its nearest centroid.
  3. Update every centroid to the mean of its cluster.
  4. Repeat 2–3 until no point changes cluster.
  • Each step never increases J and there are finitely many partitions, so it always converges, but only to a local optimum: the start matters.
  • Limits: k must be given; assumes round, similar-size clusters; sensitive to scale (standardise) and outliers; each point belongs to one cluster only.

K-Means++ seeding ★★★

\[D(x)=\min_{\text{chosen }\mu}\ d(x,\mu)\]
distance from x to the nearest centroid already chosen
  • \(D(x)\)distance from x to the nearest centroid already chosen
\[P(x\ \text{is the next centroid})=\frac{D(x)^2}{\sum_{x'}D(x')^2}\]
far points are more likely to be picked
  • \(D(x)^2\)squared distance of x
  • \(\sum_{x'}D(x')^2\)total over all points
  1. Choose the first centroid at random (it is given in the question).
  2. For every point compute D(x)² to the nearest chosen centroid.
  3. Pick the next centroid with probability D(x)² / ΣD² (exam: take the highest).
  4. Repeat until k centroids, then run normal K-Means.
  • Her example: first A1 → ΣD² = 282 → A3 most likely (72/282 = 25.53%) → with A1, A3: ΣD² = 102 → C1 (53/102 = 51.96%).
  • Initial WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares): her manual start 67 vs K-Means++ 34; the K-Means++ start is already the final clustering (one check instead of 4 iterations). Use exact d² (17), never a rounded distance squared (4.12²).

Choosing K: elbow and silhouette ★★★

\[a(i)=\text{mean distance from }i\text{ to the other points of its own cluster}\]
cohesion
  • \(i\)the point being scored
  • \(a(i)\)cohesion: small is good
\[b(i)=\min_{\text{other clusters}}\ \text{mean distance from }i\text{ to that cluster}\]
separation from the nearest other cluster
  • \(b(i)\)separation: large is good
\[s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),\,b(i)\}}\]
silhouette of one point, from −1 to 1 (a singleton gets 0)
  • \(s(i)\)silhouette of point i
  • \(a(i)\)cohesion
  • \(b(i)\)separation
\[\bar s=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i s(i)\]
average silhouette: choose the k with the highest value
  • \(\bar s\)average silhouette
  • \(n\)number of points
  • Elbow: WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) always falls as k grows (it is 0 when k = n); choose the k after which the drop becomes small. Her example 900, 400, 150, 130, 120, 113 → drops 500, 250, 20 → k = 3. It is subjective.
  • Silhouette: near 1 = well placed, ≈ 0 = on a boundary, < 0 = probably in the wrong cluster. Her slide: a = 2, b = 5 → s = 0.6.
  • Her 1-D example {1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12}: WCSS 125.5 (k = 1), 4 (k = 2), 2.5 (k = 3) → elbow at 2; silhouette 0.85 (k = 2) vs 0.50 (k = 3) → k = 2 by both.
Her worked example★★★

Her WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) notes: for the data {1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12}, compare the clusterings k = 1, k = 2 ({1, 2, 3}, {10, 11, 12}) and k = 3 ({1, 2, 3}, {10, 11}, {12}) by WCSS and average silhouette.

Solution

Hierarchical clustering ★★★

  • Agglomerative (bottom-up, common): every point starts as its own cluster; repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one remains.
  • Divisive (top-down, rare): start with one cluster containing everything and keep splitting; expensive.
  • The dendrogram records the merges and their heights; cutting it at a height gives the clusters, so k is chosen after seeing the structure (unlike K-Means).
  • Cost: naive agglomerative O(n³) time and O(n²) memory vs K-Means O(n·k·d) per iteration, so K-Means suits large n.

Association rules and Apriori ★★★

\[\text{sup}(X)=\frac{\#\text{transactions containing }X}{N}\]
how often the itemset appears
  • \(X\)an itemset, e.g. {Bread, Milk}
  • \(N\)total number of transactions
\[\text{conf}(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{\text{sup}(X\cup Y)}{\text{sup}(X)}\]
how often Y appears when X does
  • \(X\Rightarrow Y\)the rule “if X then Y”
  • \(X\cup Y\)both itemsets together
\[\text{lift}(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{\text{conf}(X\Rightarrow Y)}{\text{sup}(Y)}\]
1 = independent, > 1 = positive association, < 1 = negative (substitutes)
  • \(\text{sup}(Y)\)support of Y on its own
\[\text{conviction}=\frac{1-\text{sup}(Y)}{1-\text{conf}(X\Rightarrow Y)}\]
infinite when the rule never fails
  • \(\text{conf}(X\Rightarrow Y)\)confidence of the rule
  • \(\text{sup}(Y)\)support of Y
  • Apriori property: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, so a candidate with any infrequent subset is pruned without counting.
  • Steps: count 1-itemsets → keep those ≥ minimum support (L₁) → join to make candidates C₂ → prune → count → keep L₂ → repeat until no candidates → form rules with confidence ≥ minimum confidence.
  • Her example (minimum support 0.6): L₁ = Bread, Milk, Diaper (0.8), Beer (0.6); L₂ = {Bread, Milk}, {Bread, Diaper}, {Milk, Diaper}, {Diaper, Beer}; {Bread, Milk, Diaper} has 0.4 and fails.
  • FP-Growth (Frequent-Pattern Growth) compresses the data into an FP-tree (Frequent-Pattern Tree) in exactly two scans and mines it without generating candidates (fast on dense data; the tree must fit in memory). Apriori scans once per level.

Her slides 40–43: T1 {Bread, Milk}, T2 {Bread, Diaper, Beer, Egg}, T3 {Milk, Diaper, Beer, Cola}, T4 {Bread, Milk, Diaper, Beer}, T5 {Bread, Milk, Diaper, Cola}. Find the frequent itemsets with minimum support 0.6 and the rules with confidence ≥ 0.7.

Solution

PCA: principal component analysis ★★★

\[\text{PC}_1=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\dots+a_pX_p\]
each component is a weighted mix of all features
  • \(X_1,\dots,X_p\)the original standardised features
  • \(a_1,\dots,a_p\)their weights (loadings)
\[\text{explained variance ratio}_i=\frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j\lambda_j}\]
share of the total variance carried by component i
  • \(\lambda_i\)variance carried by component i (its eigenvalue)
  • \(\sum_j\lambda_j\)total variance
  • PCA (Principal Component Analysis) builds new uncorrelated variables (components). PC1 (First Principal Component) has the most variance, PC2 (Second Principal Component) the next and is orthogonal to PC1, and so on. 5 features give up to 5 PCs (Principal Components); reduction happens when we keep fewer.
  • Her example: 60, 25, 10, 4, 1% → cumulative 60, 85, 95% → keep 3 PCs for 95%. With a 0.95 target and cumulative 55, 80, 92, 97, 100% → keep 4.
  • Steps: standardise → find the directions → rank by explained variance → keep enough (90–95%) → project the data. PCA is feature extraction (new features), not selection; the components are hard to interpret.

Semi-supervised and reinforcement learning ★★★

  • Semi-supervised: a few labels + many unlabelled rows (500 labelled + 9,500 unlabelled car images). Assumptions: smoothness (nearby points share labels), cluster (points in one group share a label; boundaries pass through low-density regions), manifold. Self-training: train on labelled data → predict the unlabelled → keep only confident pseudo-labels (cat 99%: keep; cat 52%: ignore) → retrain. Risk: confirmation bias, a confidently wrong label is reinforced.
  • Reinforcement learning: an agent acts in an environment and learns from rewards, not labelled answers. MDP (Markov Decision Process) (S, A, P, R, γ): states, actions, transitions P(s′ | s, a), rewards, discount γ (small = short-sighted, large = values the future). A policy π(a | s) maximises the long-term reward.
  • Exploration vs exploitation: try something new vs use the best known action. V(s) = value of a state; Q(s, a) = value of an action in a state (Q(red light, stop) ≫ Q(red light, accelerate)). Q-learning learns Q and takes the max-Q action.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the K-Means algorithm. Does it always converge? State its limitations.

Answer, as you would write it

K-Means splits n points into k clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squares \(J=\sum_i\sum_{x\in C_i}\lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2\).

  1. Choose k initial centroids.
  2. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
  3. Update each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until no point changes cluster.

Convergence: both steps can only lower (or keep) J and there are finitely many partitions, so it always stops; but it may stop at a local optimum that depends on the starting centroids.

Limitations: k must be chosen in advance; sensitive to initialisation, outliers and feature scale; assumes round clusters of similar size; hard assignment only.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the K-Means++ initialisation and why it improves K-Means.

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Pick the first centroid uniformly at random.
  2. For every point, compute D(x), the distance to the nearest centroid chosen so far.
  3. Pick the next centroid with probability \(\frac{D(x)^2}{\sum D(x')^2}\), so far-away points are favoured.
  4. Repeat until k centroids are chosen, then run the usual K-Means.

Why better: the seeds are spread across different natural groups instead of two landing in one cluster. The starting WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) is lower (her example: 34 vs 67), K-Means needs fewer iterations (1 check vs 4), and the expected result is within O(log k) of the optimum.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the elbow method and the silhouette score for choosing k.

Answer, as you would write it

Elbow method: run K-Means for k = 1, 2, 3, … and plot WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) against k. WCSS always decreases, so choose the k at the "elbow", where adding another cluster gives only a small drop (900, 400, 150, 130 → k = 3). It is simple but subjective.

Silhouette: for each point, a = mean distance to its own cluster and b = mean distance to the nearest other cluster; \(s=\frac{b-a}{\max(a,b)}\) lies in [−1, 1]. Values near 1 mean well-separated clusters, near 0 a boundary point, negative a wrong assignment. Choose the k with the highest average silhouette.

Theory★★★5 marks

Differentiate agglomerative and divisive hierarchical clustering. What is a dendrogram?

Answer, as you would write it

Agglomerative (bottom-up): start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one cluster remains. Common and simple.

Divisive (top-down): start with all points in one cluster and repeatedly split until each point is alone. Needs a splitting method at every step, so it is expensive and rare.

A dendrogram is the tree diagram of the merges; the height of each join shows the distance at which the clusters merged. Cutting it horizontally at a chosen height gives the clusters (above: {A, B}, {C, D}, {E}).

Theory★★★5 marks

Define support, confidence and lift. State the Apriori property and explain how Apriori uses it.

Answer, as you would write it

Support of X = share of transactions containing X. Confidence of X ⇒ Y = sup(X ∪ Y)/sup(X), how often Y appears when X does. Lift = conf(X ⇒ Y)/sup(Y): 1 means independent, above 1 a positive association, below 1 a negative one.

Apriori property: all subsets of a frequent itemset are frequent; equivalently, if an itemset is infrequent, all its supersets are infrequent.

Apriori builds frequent itemsets level by level: frequent 1-itemsets are joined into candidate 2-itemsets, any candidate with an infrequent subset is pruned without scanning the data, the rest are counted, and the process repeats. Rules are then formed from the frequent itemsets and kept if their confidence is high enough.

Theory★★★4 marks

What does PCA (Principal Component Analysis) do? How is the number of components chosen? Why is PCA called feature extraction, not feature selection?

Answer, as you would write it

PCA transforms correlated features into new, uncorrelated variables called principal components; PC1 (First Principal Component) captures the largest variance, PC2 (Second Principal Component) the next largest (orthogonal to PC1), and so on.

The number kept is chosen from the cumulative explained variance λᵢ/Σλ, typically enough to retain 90–95% (60, 25, 10% → 3 components give 95%).

It is extraction because each component is a new combination of all original features; selection would keep a subset of the original features unchanged.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the components of a Markov decision process in reinforcement learning, the role of γ, and the exploration–exploitation trade-off.

Answer, as you would write it

In RL (Reinforcement Learning) an agent interacts with an environment: in state s it takes action a, receives reward r and moves to a new state. It learns a policy π(a | s) that maximises long-term reward, without labelled correct actions.

MDP (Markov Decision Process) (S, A, P, R, γ): S = states (car approaching a red light), A = actions (brake, accelerate), P(s′ | s, a) = transition probabilities, R = rewards (safe stop +, collision −), γ = discount factor.

γ: a small γ makes the agent care about immediate rewards; a large γ makes it value future rewards (planning ahead).

Exploration vs exploitation: exploring tries new actions to discover better ones (a new restaurant); exploiting uses the best action known so far (the usual restaurant). A good agent balances both.

Theory★★★4 marks

What is semi-supervised learning? Explain self-training and its main risk.

Answer, as you would write it

Semi-supervised learning trains on a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set (500 labelled and 9,500 unlabelled images), assuming nearby points or points in the same cluster share a label.

Self-training: train on the labelled data → predict the unlabelled data → add only high-confidence predictions as pseudo-labels (cat 99%: keep; cat 52%: ignore) → retrain, and repeat.

Risk: confirmation bias: a confidently wrong pseudo-label is learned and reinforced. Use strict thresholds and a clean validation set.

Analytical★★★4 marks

Why does K-Means++ give a lower initial WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) than a manual start, and does K-Means always find the best clustering?

Answer, as you would write it

D² sampling favours points far from the chosen centroids, so the seeds land in different natural groups instead of two in the same cluster. Each point is then already close to a centroid, giving a compact start (her example: 34 vs 67).

K-Means always converges, because J never increases and the number of partitions is finite, but only to a local optimum that depends on the start. That is why K-Means++ or several random restarts are used.

Analytical★★★3 marks

WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) keeps decreasing as k increases. Why not simply choose a large k?

Answer, as you would write it

More centroids always sit closer to the points, so WCSS can only fall, reaching 0 when k = n (every point its own cluster), which tells us nothing. Choose the elbow, where an extra cluster stops giving a large drop, and confirm with the silhouette, which penalises splitting a real cluster.

Analytical★★★3 marks

For a dataset, k = 3 gives a lower WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) than k = 2, but its average silhouette is 0.50 vs 0.85. Which k should be chosen?

Answer, as you would write it

k = 2. WCSS always drops when k increases, so the lower WCSS at k = 3 is expected and proves nothing. The silhouette compares cohesion with separation: 0.85 means two well-separated groups, while 0.50 shows k = 3 split a real cluster (points like 11 and 12 sit almost on a boundary).

Analytical★★★3 marks

The rule {Bread} ⇒ {Coffee} has confidence 0.9, but 90% of all customers buy coffee anyway. Is the rule useful?

Answer, as you would write it

No. Lift = conf / sup(Coffee) = 0.9 / 0.9 = 1, so buying bread does not change the chance of buying coffee: the items are independent. Confidence looks high only because coffee is popular. Lift (or conviction) shows whether the association is real.

Analytical★★★3 marks

In her Apriori example, why is {Milk, Diaper, Beer} never even counted?

Answer, as you would write it

By the Apriori property every subset of a frequent itemset must be frequent. {Milk, Beer} appears in only 2 of 5 transactions (support 0.4 < 0.6), so it is not in L₂, and any superset containing it, such as {Milk, Diaper, Beer}, is pruned without scanning the data.

13

Time series: components, stationarity, AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA

PDF: Time Series (59 slides, class 1 + self-study class 2) · Word: Time Series notes · she said: "not many questions, but small 1–2 mark equation math will come"

Math: small forecasts (promised)TheoryAnalytical★★★

What a time series is ★★★

  • Time series = observations recorded in time order (daily temperature, monthly sales, hourly electricity use): Y₁, Y₂, …, Yt. Order matters and earlier values influence later ones.
  • Cross-sectional data = many observations at one time (500 salaries today); order does not matter. Shuffling a time series destroys its pattern.
  • Why analyse: understand change, find trend and seasonality, forecast, plan, detect anomalies. Forecasts are estimates, not guarantees; uncertainty grows with the horizon.
  • Workflow: plot → look for trend, seasonality, unusual events → clean → choose a model → fit and evaluate → forecast and monitor. "Do not start with ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) immediately."

Components: trend, seasonal, cyclical, irregular ★★★

\[Y_t=T_t+S_t+C_t+I_t\]
additive model: the seasonal swing has a constant size (±100 units every December)
  • \(Y_t\)value at time t
  • \(T_t\)trend
  • \(S_t\)seasonal effect
  • \(C_t\)cyclical effect
  • \(I_t\)irregular part (noise)
\[Y_t=T_t\times S_t\times C_t\times I_t\]
multiplicative model: the swing grows with the level (December always 30% higher)
  • \(T_t,\ S_t,\ C_t,\ I_t\)the same components, now multiplied (Sₜ = 1.3 means 30% above trend)
\[Y_t=100+30+15+5=150\]
her additive example (T = 100, S = 30, C = 15, I = 5)
  • \(100\)trend
  • \(30\)seasonal effect
  • \(15\)cyclical effect
  • \(5\)irregular part
  • Trend T: the long-term direction (online sales rising for years).
  • Seasonal S: a repeating pattern with a known, fixed period (retail peaks every December; period 12 for monthly data, 4 for quarterly).
  • Cyclical C: longer rises and falls with no fixed period (business cycles, recessions). "Summer every year = seasonal; a recession = cyclical."
  • Irregular I: random noise and shocks (strikes, disasters). The components are estimated by decomposition.

Lag, autocorrelation, ACF and PACF ★★★

\[Y_{t-k}\]
lag k: the value k periods earlier
  • \(t\)current time
  • \(k\)how many periods back
\[\rho_k=\operatorname{Corr}(Y_t,\ Y_{t-k})\]
autocorrelation at lag k: > 0 high follows high, < 0 alternating, ≈ 0 little linear memory
  • \(\rho_k\)autocorrelation at lag k
  • \(\operatorname{Corr}\)Pearson correlation
  • Her lag example: Jan 100, Feb 110, Mar 125, Apr 140. For April, Yt = 140, lag 1 = 125, lag 2 = 110, lag 3 = 100.
  • ACF = autocorrelation at every lag (her example 0.82, 0.65, 0.44, 0.20, 0.05: memory fades). Spikes beyond the confidence bounds are significant; a very slow decay hints at non-stationarity.
  • PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function) = the direct correlation with lag k after removing the effect of the shorter lags. At lag 1, ACF = PACF.

Stationarity, the ADF test and differencing ★★★

\[E(Y_t)=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=\sigma^2\]
weak stationarity: constant mean and variance over time
  • \(E(Y_t)\)expected value (mean) at time t
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)\)variance at time t
\[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t-k})\ \text{depends only on }k\]
and the autocovariance depends only on the lag
  • \(\operatorname{Cov}\)covariance
  • \(k\)lag
\[\nabla Y_t=Y_t-Y_{t-1}\]
first difference: removes a linear trend; difference again (d = 2) for a curved trend
  • \(\nabla Y_t\)first difference at time t
  • \(Y_{t-1}\)previous value
  • Stationary: 100, 103, 98, 101, 99, 102 (wobbles around a fixed level). Non-stationary: 100, 110, 125, 140, 160, 180 (trend). Causes: trend, changing variance, seasonality, structural breaks.
  • ADF (Augmented Dickey–Fuller) test: H₀ = unit root (non-stationary), H₁ = stationary; p < 0.05 → evidence of stationarity. Also look at the plot and the ACF (Autocorrelation Function).
  • Her differencing: 100, 110, 125, 140, 155 → 10, 15, 15, 15 (much more stable). Too much differencing adds noise and damages the series. The number of differencing rounds is the d of ARIMA(p, d, q) (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average).

AR, MA, ARMA and ARIMA models ★★★

\[Y_t=c+\phi_1Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\]
AR(1) (Autoregressive): today depends on yesterday's value
  • \(c\)constant (intercept)
  • \(\phi_1\)AR coefficient: weight on the previous value
  • \(Y_{t-1}\)previous value
  • \(\varepsilon_t\)today's random shock: 0 on average, so set to 0 when forecasting
\[Y_t=c+\phi_1Y_{t-1}+\phi_2Y_{t-2}+\dots+\phi_pY_{t-p}+\varepsilon_t\]
AR(p): uses the last p values
  • \(p\)number of past values used
  • \(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_p\)their weights
\[Y_t=\mu+\varepsilon_t+\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}\]
MA(1) (Moving Average): today depends on yesterday's shock (innovation)
  • \(\mu\)mean of the series
  • \(\theta_1\)MA coefficient: weight on the previous shock
  • \(\varepsilon_{t-1}\)previous shock (last forecast error)
\[\varepsilon_{t-1}=Y_{t-1}-\hat Y_{t-1}\]
the innovation = last actual − last forecast
  • \(\hat Y_{t-1}\)what was forecast for the previous period
\[Y_t=c+\phi_1Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t+\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}\]
ARMA(1,1) (Autoregressive Moving Average): both, for a stationary series
  • \(\phi_1\)AR weight on the previous value
  • \(\theta_1\)MA weight on the previous shock
\[\text{ARIMA}(p,d,q)=\text{ARMA}(p,q)\ \text{on the series differenced }d\text{ times}\]
for non-stationary data
  • \(p\)AR order (past values)
  • \(d\)number of differencing rounds
  • \(q\)MA order (past shocks)
  • To forecast: set the future shock εt = 0 and plug in the known past values and past errors.
  • Her results: AR(1) 10 + 0.8(100) = 90; AR(2) 5 + 0.6(100) + 0.2(90) = 83; MA(1) 100 + 0.5(10) = 105; class activity AR(2) 10 + 0.7(120) + 0.2(100) = 114.
  • MA here means "moving-average of past shocks", not the ordinary moving average of past values.
AR(p)MA(q)
UsesPast values Yt−1, …Past shocks εt−1, …
Orderp = number of value lagsq = number of shock lags
ACF (Autocorrelation Function)Tails off slowlyCuts off after lag q
PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function)Cuts off after lag pTails off slowly

ARMA: both ACF and PACF tail off.

MathPredicted★★★10 marks
  1. Identify the model Yt = 12 + 0.5Yt−1 + 0.3Yt−2 + εt and forecast Yt when Yt−1 = 80 and Yt−2 = 70. [3]

(b) Innovation εt−1 = 58 − 54 = 4.

(c)

The first differences 15, 18, 21, 24 still rise, so one round is not enough; the second differences 3, 3, 3 are constant (d = 2).

(d) \(Y_t=T_t+S_t+C_t+I_t=120+(-15)+8+2=115\).

Answer, as you would write it
Theory★★★5 marks

Explain the four components of a time series with examples. Differentiate the additive and multiplicative models.

Answer, as you would write it

Trend (T): the long-term upward or downward movement, e.g. online sales growing every year.

Seasonal (S): a pattern repeating with a fixed, known period, e.g. retail sales peaking every December.

Cyclical (C): longer rises and falls with no fixed period, e.g. business cycles and recessions.

Irregular (I): random, unpredictable variation, e.g. a strike or a flood.

Additive \(Y_t=T_t+S_t+C_t+I_t\): the seasonal effect is a constant amount (+100 units each December). Multiplicative \(Y_t=T_t\times S_t\times C_t\times I_t\): the seasonal effect is a proportion, so the swings grow as the level grows (+30% each December).

Theory★★★5 marks

What is a stationary time series? How can stationarity be checked, and how is a non-stationary series made stationary?

Answer, as you would write it

A series is (weakly) stationary when its statistical behaviour does not change over time: a constant mean, a constant variance, and an autocovariance that depends only on the lag. Example: 100, 103, 98, 101, 99, 102.

Checking: plot the series (look for trend or changing spread); look at the ACF (Autocorrelation Function) (a very slow decay suggests non-stationarity); run the ADF (Augmented Dickey–Fuller) test, where H₀ is a unit root (non-stationary): p < 0.05 rejects it, giving evidence of stationarity.

Fixing: differencing, \(\nabla Y_t=Y_t-Y_{t-1}\): 100, 110, 125, 140, 155 → 10, 15, 15, 15. Repeat (d = 2) if a trend remains; transformations such as log can stabilise a growing variance.

Theory★★★5 marks

Differentiate AR (Autoregressive) and MA (Moving Average) models. What are ARMA (Autoregressive Moving Average) and ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average)? Explain p, d and q.

Answer, as you would write it

AR(p) (autoregressive): today's value is a linear combination of its own past values, \(Y_t=c+\phi_1Y_{t-1}+\dots+\phi_pY_{t-p}+\varepsilon_t\).

MA(q) (moving average): today's value depends on past forecast errors (shocks), \(Y_t=\mu+\varepsilon_t+\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}+\dots+\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}\).

ARMA(p, q) combines both, for a stationary series. ARIMA(p, d, q) first differences a non-stationary series d times ("I" = integrated) and then fits ARMA(p, q).

p = number of AR lags (past values), d = number of differencing rounds, q = number of MA lags (past errors).

Theory★★★5 marks

Differentiate time-series and cross-sectional data. Define lag, ACF (Autocorrelation Function) and PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function).

Answer, as you would write it

Time-series data are observations of one variable in time order (monthly sales 2024–2026); the order matters and neighbouring values are related. Cross-sectional data are many observations at one time (500 salaries today); the order does not matter.

Lag k: the value k periods earlier, Yt−k (for April 140: lag 1 = March 125).

ACF: the correlation between Yt and Yt−k for each lag k; it shows how long the memory lasts.

PACF: the correlation between Yt and Yt−k after removing the effect of the shorter lags; it shows the direct effect of lag k.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A series' ACF (Autocorrelation Function) decays gradually while its PACF (Partial Autocorrelation Function) has significant spikes only at lags 1 and 2. Which model should be tried, and why?

Answer, as you would write it

AR(2) (Autoregressive). For an AR(p) process the PACF cuts off after lag p (direct effects exist only up to p), while the ACF tails off because each value carries the effect of earlier values. Spikes at lags 1 and 2 → p = 2. (If the ACF cut off at 2 and the PACF tailed off, it would be MA(2) (Moving Average).)

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why do AR (Autoregressive), MA (Moving Average) and ARMA (Autoregressive Moving Average) models need a stationary series? What does a slowly decaying ACF (Autocorrelation Function) suggest?

Answer, as you would write it

These models assume that the relationships they learn (mean, variance, the effect of each lag) stay the same over time; only then can patterns from the past be used to forecast the future. With a trend, the mean keeps moving and the fitted coefficients are unreliable.

A slowly decaying ACF means values are correlated with values far in the past, usually because of a trend: the series is likely non-stationary and should be differenced.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Why can't time-series rows be shuffled randomly, as in an ordinary train/test split?

Answer, as you would write it

In a time series each value depends on the previous ones (autocorrelation), and trend and seasonality only exist in the time order. Shuffling destroys these patterns and lets the model "see the future" during training (data leakage). The split must be chronological: train on the past, test on the later period.

Analytical★★★3 marks

Is the MA (Moving Average) model the same as taking a moving average of past values? Explain.

Answer, as you would write it

No. An ordinary moving average smooths past values ((Yt−1 + Yt−2 + Yt−3)/3). The MA(q) model uses past shocks, the forecast errors εt−1 = Yt−1 − Ŷt−1: for example 100 + 0.5(110 − 100) = 105. It models how a surprise last period carries into this period.

Analytical★★★2 marks

Why is excessive differencing harmful, and why does forecast uncertainty grow with the horizon?

Answer, as you would write it

Each extra difference removes information and adds noise (it can create artificial negative correlation), so the model fits worse.

Forecasts further ahead are built on earlier forecasts instead of real values, so errors accumulate; new shocks between now and then are unknown.

14

Applications, ethics and research directions

Lecture note: Applications, Ethics, and Research Directions (3 pages) · linked to her research-paper project (Quiz 4)

TheoryAnalytical: scenarios★★★

Principles of research ethics ★★★

Research ethics = the principles for collecting data, running experiments, analysing and publishing honestly, reliably, transparently and respectfully.

  1. Privacy and confidentiality: collect only what is needed, store it securely, never publish identities (no patient names or addresses).
  2. Informed consent and ethics approval: tell participants the purpose, use and risks; a student mental-health survey needs ethics-committee approval.
  3. Academic honesty and integrity: no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism.
  4. Proper citation of methods (Random Forest), datasets and others' ideas.
  5. Transparency and reproducibility: report the dataset, preprocessing, train/test split and metrics behind a "98% accuracy" claim.
  6. Fair reporting: report all results, not only favourable ones (all 5 datasets, not the best 3), to avoid publication bias.
  7. Ethical use of AI (Artificial Intelligence) tools: verify AI output, take responsibility, disclose use according to policy (e.g. ChatGPT for English editing).
  8. Authorship and publication ethics: only real contributors are authors; no duplicate publication, salami slicing, gift authorship or hidden conflicts of interest.
  9. Ethical implications of findings: discuss risks and limits (face recognition with unequal error rates across groups).

Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism ★★★

MeaningExample
FabricationInventing data or results that were never obtainedWriting survey responses that nobody gave
FalsificationManipulating materials, methods or results so the record is untrueReporting 95% accuracy when the model achieved 87%; dropping inconvenient data points
PlagiarismUsing others' ideas, words or work without creditCopying paragraphs from a paper without citation
Unethical publication practiceMeaning
Duplicate publicationPublishing the same work twice
Salami slicingSplitting one study into many small papers
Gift authorshipAdding an author who did not contribute (a senior colleague)
Undisclosed conflict of interestHiding funding or links that could bias the work
Theory★★★5 marks

Explain fabrication, falsification and plagiarism with examples. Why are they serious in data analytics research?

Answer, as you would write it

Fabrication is inventing data or results that were never collected, e.g. filling in survey answers that no respondent gave.

Falsification is manipulating data, methods or results so that the record is untrue, e.g. reporting 95% accuracy when the model achieved 87%, or deleting data points that weaken the result.

Plagiarism is presenting someone else's ideas, words, code or results as one's own without credit, e.g. copying a paper's paragraphs or a GitHub model without citation.

They are serious because decisions, policies and later research are built on published results; false or stolen work misleads others, wastes resources and destroys trust in the researcher and the field.

Theory★★★5 marks

Explain any five principles of research ethics for a data analytics study.

Answer, as you would write it
  1. Privacy and confidentiality: collect only necessary data, store it securely, remove identities before publishing.
  2. Informed consent and approval: participants know the purpose, use and risks; sensitive studies get ethics-committee approval.
  3. Integrity: no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism.
  4. Transparency and reproducibility: describe the data, preprocessing, split and metrics so others can repeat the work.
  5. Fair reporting: report all results, including negative ones, to avoid publication bias.
Theory★★★4 marks

Explain duplicate publication, salami slicing, gift authorship and undisclosed conflicts of interest.

Answer, as you would write it

Duplicate publication: publishing the same study, or substantially the same results, in more than one venue.

Salami slicing: splitting one study into several small papers to increase the publication count.

Gift authorship: listing someone as an author who did not make a real contribution (e.g. a senior colleague added for prestige).

Undisclosed conflict of interest: hiding funding or personal links (e.g. the company whose product is evaluated) that could bias the research.

Analytical★★★5 marks

Identify the ethical problem in each case and justify: (a) a student reports results on 3 of 5 datasets because the other 2 were poor; (b) a researcher adds a senior professor who did no work as co-author; (c) a model's 87% accuracy is written as 95%; (d) a hospital study publishes patients' names with their diagnoses.

Answer, as you would write it

(a) Unfair reporting / publication bias: hiding unfavourable results gives a falsely positive picture of the method; all five datasets must be reported.

(b) Gift authorship: authorship must reflect real contribution; adding a non-contributor misrepresents who did the work.

(c) Falsification: the result was changed, so the research record is untrue.

(d) Breach of privacy and confidentiality: identities must be removed and data stored securely; patients did not consent to being identified.

Analytical★★★3 marks

A student uses ChatGPT to write parts of a research paper and to suggest references. Is this ethical? What must the student do?

Answer, as you would write it

It can be acceptable for help such as English editing, but the researcher remains fully responsible. The student must verify every statement and reference (AI (Artificial Intelligence) tools can invent citations), must not present AI-generated content as original analysis, and must disclose the use according to the institution's or journal's policy. Fake references would be fabrication.
